vector[N] y; // outcomes

data {

int<lower=1> K; // num ind predictors
int<lower=1> J; // num groups
int<lower=1> L; // num group predictors
int<lower=1,upper=J> jj[N]; // group for individual
matrix[N,K] x; // individual predictors
matrix[J,L] u; // group predictors

# you have a typo here.
#vector[N] y; // outcomes
int y[N];
}

The error massage is kinda misreading. I spent a little bit of time to debug your code.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using STAN on very tall and wide data
messages.body_plain:
That's a pretty broad request!  What specifically are
you trying to do?

Stan can encode a lot of the models popular in machine
learning.  Although it scales reasonably well, it isn't
going to compete with large custom implementations.

There are no sparse data types built in (though see the
manual description of LDA for how to encode them).

There are no online algorithms yet, but Andrew's very
keen on developing and implementing them, so expect to
see more scalable methods, including online (data partitioning)
methods in six months to a year's time.

- Bob

Linas

On Tuesday, April 1, 2014 10:13:23 AM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:
> Can anybody suggest how to add constrains different than just upper/lower bounds to a model in Stan.  Specifically my model (2-compartmental PK model in closed form) may be expressed as:
> A*exp(-k1*time)+B*exp(-k2*time)+C*exp(-k3*time)
> where k1,2,3>=0, A,B,C are functions of k1,2,3.
> I need to enforce constraints on parameters to make sure that model has non negative values.  Or maybe there is another way of dealing with this?

Do you mean that

A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time) + C * exp(-k3 * time) > 0

or that A, B, C > 0? If the latter, I would tend to write

A <- exp(log_A);

and make log_A the function of k1,k2,k3. If A can be negative but the whole expression has to be positive, I would again probably model the log of it. Another way would be to do something like

exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time)) / exp(-k3 * time)> C;
  ...
}

Ben

messages.subject: Integrating out Censored Values
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I had a couple questions about handling missing data in Stan.  I have a problem that involves a potentially large about of non-ignorable missing data (something like censored data with an unknown censoring point).  My understanding is that the simplest way to handle missing data is to treat the missing data as parameters and jointly model all parameters and missing data.  However, I'm worried that this will be too costly given the amount of missing data.

Ideally I would integrate out the censored data directly but the integral has no closed form so my questions are:

1) Is there any way to include an integral in the posterior that is evaluated numerically?  I understand that the numerical evaluations (and numerical gradient calculations)
might be slow but my guess is that it might be faster than full imputation.

2) If not what reasonable alternatives might there be?  If I do try to do full imputation, are there computational tradeoffs I should keep in mind?  Is there anyway to impute missing data in a Gibbs step, separate from the HMC parameter updates?  Might this be faster than jointly proposing values for all parameters and missing data?

Thanks for any insight!

I've tried re-parameterizing my model using the multivariate Matt trick, and I must be missing something, as it runs around 4.5 times as slow and has over 6 times fewer effective samples for a reduction in Neff_S of over twentyfold, but the mean answers are pretty much the same. Model in Cholesky form
Model in Matt trick form
R file with sample data, functions, calls to the models, and comparative statistics.

On Sunday, March 30, 2014 12:07:53 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Saturday, March 29, 2014 8:48:42 PM UTC-4, Avraham Adler wrote:
> > If you note my original post, I fixed the name.
> >
> > And Dr. Goodrich, I apologize profusely for not originally ascribing credit properly.
>
> Not a big deal. The real credit should go to Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe but Bob and I have long since given up on being able to spell all that (hence the LKJ).
>
> Anyway, the broader point here is that calculating a matrix decomposition of a parameterized matrix in Stan is expensive, in part because the number of operations depends on the cube of the number of rows and in part because Stan has to use its auto-diff mechanism to compute the derivatives (which involves a chain rule whose number of links also depends on the cube of the number of rows) with respect to each scalar parameter. So if you do something like
>
> cholesky_decompose( diag_matrix(scales) * correlation_matrix * diag_matrix(scales) )
>
> or
>
> cholesky decompose( variance * correlation matrix )
>
> the cholesky_decompose() function just sees a square matrix and does not recognize that these are equivalent to
>
> diag_matrix(scales) * cholesky_decompose(correlation_matrix)
>
> and
>
> sqrt(variance) * choleksy_decompose(correlation_matrix)
>
> respectively (although as Philippe pointed out, this particular trick only applies with a diagonal matrix or a scalar).
>
> However, you ultimately want something equivalent which does not entail taking an expensive Cholesky decomposition of a correlation matrix. The attachment constructs and L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ with shape parameter eta. So, if you use that, then the above expressions are equivalent to
>
> diag_matrix(scales) * L
>
> and
>
> sqrt(variance) * L
>
> But wait, there's more! If something is getting a multivariate normal prior (or more generally anything in the elliptical distribution family), then you don't want to actually use of the multi_normal functions (ideally, those should only be used for likelihoods of data). You can make Pars a local or transformed parameter that is a function of the primitive parameter vector z via the multivariate Matt trick:
>
> z ~ normal(0,1);
>
> This way avoids having to solve a triangular system of equations inside one of the multi_normal functions. All that said, none of this makes much difference when dealing with a 2x2 covariance matrix, but it is much better when the dimension of the covariance matrix is large.
>
> Ben
>

messages.body_plain:
On Apr 1, 2014, at 8:44 PM, Alexander Franks <afr...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi all,
>
> I had a couple questions about handling missing data in Stan.  I have a problem that involves a potentially large about of non-ignorable missing data (something like censored data with an unknown censoring point).  My understanding is that the simplest way to handle missing data is to treat the missing data as parameters and jointly model all parameters and missing data.  However, I'm worried that this will be too costly given the amount of missing data.
>
> Ideally I would integrate out the censored data directly but the integral has no closed form so my questions are:
>
> 1) Is there any way to include an integral in the posterior that is evaluated numerically?  I understand that the numerical evaluations (and numerical gradient calculations)
> might be slow but my guess is that it might be faster than full imputation.

I'm afraid not.  We'll soon have integrators built in to solve
initial value ODE problems, but that won't be for a few months.

Then we may think about more implicit ways of defining functions,
because several people have asked for it and some of our dev team's
interested.

> 2) If not what reasonable alternatives might there be?

There aren't any other alternatives built into Stan.

How much data do you have and how complicated is the model?

> If I do try to do full imputation, are there computational tradeoffs I should keep in mind?

Just parameterizations and vectorization --- what we talk about
in the optimization and reparameterization chapters of the manual.

> Is there anyway to impute missing data in a Gibbs step, separate from the HMC parameter updates?

Not presently.

> Might this be faster than jointly proposing values for all parameters and missing data?

Probably not.  HMC is pretty fast, but it can definitely be beat
by exact conjugate Gibbs in some cases, at least in lower dimensions.

But we haven't done any serious evaluations of blocking, for example
as suggested by Radford Neal in his MCMC Handbook paper on HMC.

- Bob

On Apr 1, 2014, at 8:28 PM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks, Ben.  How to allow situations such as A,B>0 but C<0?  The plasma concentration profile may be represented as a sum of exponentials with positive and negative coefficients.

Unless you know something about the constraints on values,
the bounds on C given A and B are data dependent.  You can
just do the algebra, though:

  0 < A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time) + C * exp(-k3 * time)

iff

  -[A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time)] < C * exp(-k3 * time)

iff

  -[A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time)] / exp(-k3 * time) < C

So you need to take the lower bound for C to be

  max_{k1,k2,k3,time}
    -[A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time)]
    / exp(-k3 * time)

It may not actually be possible to calculate this in Stan, because
you need the bound at the point you declare C, at least to support
the direct constraint approach.

>
> I think when I am done with this model I am willing to donate the model (standard 2-compartmental) along with anti-cancer drug data (documented in open literature) as an example of PK modeling in Stan.

Thanks.  That'd be great, and we'd of course provide
attribution and proper credit!

- Bob

>
> Linas
> On 4/1/2014 12:34 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>> In this case, I think you will be fine. Ultimately, you can use the lognormal density, so just do
>>
>> y ~ lognormal(log_model,sigma);
>>
>> but first you have to create the log_model array. In your case,
>>
>> A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time) + C * exp(-k3 * time)
>> ==
>> exp(log_A) * exp(-k1 * time) + exp(log_B) * exp(-k2 * time)+exp(log_C) * exp(-k3 * time)
>> ==
>> exp(log_A - k1 * time) + exp(log_B - k2 * time) + exp(log_C - k3 * time)
>>
>> Thus, log_model is in the form of a log_sum_exp() of a vector of length 3 (which also helps with the numerical stability of this thing):
>>
>> for(time in 1:8) {
>>   vector[3] temp;
>>   temp[1] <- log_A - k1 * time;
>>   temp[2] <- log_B - k2 * time;
>>   temp[3] <- log_C - k3 * time;
>>   log_model[time] <- log_sum_exp(temp);
>> }
>> y ~ lognormal(log_model, sigma);
>>
>> You just need to declare log_A, log_B, and log_C as parameters rather than A, B, and C.
>>
>> Ben
>>
>> On Tuesday, April 1, 2014 12:17:21 PM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:
>> Thanks Ben,
>>
>> I meant A*exp(-k1*time)+B*exp(-k2*time)+C*exp(-k3*time) >=0.
>>

>>     model <- A*exp(-k1*time)+B*exp(-k2*time)+C*exp(-k3*time);

>> }

On Apr 1, 2014, at 11:39 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Michael Betancourt has a paper forthcoming with Mark Girolami
> where they analyze the "centered" parameterizations in a univariate
> setting for HMC (I don't think they did multivariate), and like others in
> the previous literature for Metropolis and Gibbs, found that how effective
> it is depends on the amount of data.  The reparameterization is most
> effective with less data.
>
> As to your particular models, I think you want Ben's input!
> It looks similar to the manual as far as I can see.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On Apr 1, 2014, at 9:00 PM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> I've tried re-parameterizing my model using the multivariate Matt trick, and I must be missing something, as it runs around 4.5 times as slow and has over 6 times fewer effective samples for a reduction in Neff_S of over twentyfold, but the mean answers are pretty much the same. I've attached three files:
>>

>> 	* Model in Cholesky form
>> 	* Model in Matt trick form
>> 	* R file with sample data, functions, calls to the models, and comparative statistics.

>> I've probably made an error in interpreting page 183 of the manual (v2.2.0) and any corrections would surely be appreciated
>>
>> Thank you,
>>
>> Avi
>>
>>
>>
>>
>> On Sunday, March 30, 2014 12:07:53 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>> On Saturday, March 29, 2014 8:48:42 PM UTC-4, Avraham Adler wrote:
>> If you note my original post, I fixed the name.
>>
>> And Dr. Goodrich, I apologize profusely for not originally ascribing credit properly.
>>
>> Not a big deal. The real credit should go to Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe but Bob and I have long since given up on being able to spell all that (hence the LKJ).
>>
>> Anyway, the broader point here is that calculating a matrix decomposition of a parameterized matrix in Stan is expensive, in part because the number of operations depends on the cube of the number of rows and in part because Stan has to use its auto-diff mechanism to compute the derivatives (which involves a chain rule whose number of links also depends on the cube of the number of rows) with respect to each scalar parameter. So if you do something like
>>
>> cholesky_decompose( diag_matrix(scales) * correlation_matrix * diag_matrix(scales) )
>>
>> or
>>
>> cholesky decompose( variance * correlation matrix )
>>
>> the cholesky_decompose() function just sees a square matrix and does not recognize that these are equivalent to
>>
>> diag_matrix(scales) * cholesky_decompose(correlation_matrix)
>>
>> and
>>
>> sqrt(variance) * choleksy_decompose(correlation_matrix)
>>
>> respectively (although as Philippe pointed out, this particular trick only applies with a diagonal matrix or a scalar).
>>
>> However, you ultimately want something equivalent which does not entail taking an expensive Cholesky decomposition of a correlation matrix. The attachment constructs and L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ with shape parameter eta. So, if you use that, then the above expressions are equivalent to
>>
>> diag_matrix(scales) * L
>>
>> and
>>
>> sqrt(variance) * L
>>
>> But wait, there's more! If something is getting a multivariate normal prior (or more generally anything in the elliptical distribution family), then you don't want to actually use of the multi_normal functions (ideally, those should only be used for likelihoods of data). You can make Pars a local or transformed parameter that is a function of the primitive parameter vector z via the multivariate Matt trick:
>>
>> z ~ normal(0,1);
>>
>> This way avoids having to solve a triangular system of equations inside one of the multi_normal functions. All that said, none of this makes much difference when dealing with a 2x2 covariance matrix, but it is much better when the dimension of the covariance matrix is large.
>>
>> Ben
>>
>>

messages.body_plain:
That's great news.  Thanks for sharing.

And of course, to dwell on the negative, what computation
is slow in Stan compared to R?  log_determinant?  And
you're talking about doing this in the generated quantities block
and not with parameters?

And we definitely have sparse matrix operations fairly high up
on our to-do list (which is still beyond the immediate future,
I'm afraid).

- Bob

On Mar 31, 2014, at 5:48 PM, Kyle Foreman <kylef...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I've successfully run 2100 spatial units with the sparse method - it still takes a while to sample, but it's significantly faster than using multi_normal_prec() for my use case. Results will vary depending on sparsity etc of course. And as Bob notes, it's the effective sample size that's important, not the number of iterations. I find that with these tweaks I get better convergence and much lower time per effective sample than BUGS/JAGS.
>
> I've attached a little tutorial on how to use increment_log_prob() to sample the sparse matrix. It uses the same GeoBUGS Scotland lip cancer example as my original CAR thread. It's pretty thoroughly documented, so hopefully you can get the gist just by reading through.
>
> One sacrifice it makes is that it uses an estimate of the log determinant of the precision matrix instead of computing it directly. To scale it up beyond the 56 spatial units in the example, I recommend sampling the log determinant in R instead of Stan, because that step (which fortunately only has to happen once) is a couple orders of magnitude slower in Stan than R and can take quite a while once you're up to hundreds or thousands of spatial units.
>
> There may be some tricks to replicate the CAR distribution using something like the multivariate Matt trick that Ben mentions - I haven't tried that, but would be very interested to hear how it works if you test it out.
>
> Agreed that a built in distribution would be easier, but before that becomes feasible in a case like this I would think a sparse matrix object for Stan would be required.
>
>
> On Sun, Mar 30, 2014 at 6:16 PM, MT <micha...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Kyle,
>
> I was thinking of going the lp_ route next, and your comment reassures it is a fruitful endeavor. Do you speculate that the lp_ might solve the "larger" 480 spatial neighbors problem, if scaling the data up is indeed the problem? Amongst my browsing, i think i read a tangent comment about a stan bottleneck about the 'differentiation tree'
>
> As a new user of stan, i would think successful reliance on  ' ~ ' and built in distributions would be a great pedagogical aid for newcomers, as users would not have to entertain two alternatives to implement their model.
>
> I was hoping stan would successfully sample without relying on the lp_ mechanism.
> It looks like, for niche models such as these, one is forced to use lp_.
>
>
>
>
> On Sunday, March 30, 2014 8:57:48 PM UTC-4, Kyle Foreman wrote:
> Hi MT,
>
> Why are you imposing the restriction of no direct manipulation of lp__? I've had success in speeding up my CAR and MCAR models by using sparse covariance matrices for the MVN, but it requires you to write out the MVN probability explicitly by manipulating lp__ instead of using the built in probability functions.
>
> Best
> Kyle
>
> On Sunday, March 30, 2014 4:50:06 PM UTC-7, MT wrote:
> Hi all,
>
> I've been looking at past threads regarding Conditional Auto Regressive (CAR) models.
>
> (In order of relevance)
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/spatial/stan-users/S8dhFpn0Lg8/F91hZXBJmnMJ
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/spatial/stan-users/63m5A5ATzs8/LII8RuX2jI8J
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/spatial/stan-users/he7BxxHfBfk/V6s1K14nRfgJ
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/spatial/stan-users/iddShgJVwTQ/Ihes0SOy5yQJ
>
> I've tried to adapt the examples to my fake toy example with little success.
> (by adapting, i mean a naive specification without resorting to working with the lp_ directly)
>
> I've finally hit my wall, and would appreciate some help.
> Is working with lp_ the only way to practically implement this model?
>
> Problems:
> 	• The practical problem I face is the sampling is extremely slow compared to WinBUGS.
> I already have results from WinBUGS, where my attempt in Stan doesn't even return 1000 iterations when I allow 8+ hours for the running clock time.
> Further, i'd like the restriction of avoiding the use of lp_ directly
> 	• Possibly related, I get multiple stan warnings about non-symmetric covariance matrices, when I believe they are intentionally symmetric.
> covariance matrix[0,2] is 105097511.634409:0, but
> covariance matrix[2,0] is 1.05098e+008:0
>
> Background and Details:
> The model is a two stage model, where the data model is Poisson, and the log Poisson rate is linear with fixed effects and random effects
>
> Past stan examples used a "small" number of spatial neighbors, say 50.
> My toy example has 480 neighbors.
>
> Past examples used a single random effect, the spatial conditional autoregressive (CAR) effect
> My example uses two random effects (as in the Besag-York-Mollie model) one spatial CAR and the other normal
>
> Past examples estimated the spatial dependence parameter and also giving it a uniform prior
> My example fixes (doesn't estimate) the spatial dependence parameter using the reciprocal of the largest eigenvalue of some matrix.
>
> Model:
> In short, i've tried to follow Cressie and Wikle's (statistics for spatiao-temporal data) more general model specification
>
> A stylized Model Specification:
>
> O ~ poisson(mu)
> log_mu <- log(E) + alpha0 + alpha1 * x1 + ( beta1-mean(beta1) ) + beta2
> beta1 ~ MVN(0,Cov_spatial)
> beta2 ~ MVN(0,Cov_normal)
> Cov_spatial <- tau^2 * inverse(ONES - phi * H ) * DELTA
> Cov_normal <- sigma^2 * ONES
>
> Where:
> O is the response count
> mu is the poisson rate
> E is an offset
> alpha0 is the uninteresting intercept
> alpha1 is a fixed effect
> beta1 is the spatial random effect using a MVN with a spatially structured covariance (Cov_spatial)
> beta2 is the nonspatial random effect using a MVN with  covariance (Cov_normal)
>
> tau is the standard deviation for the spatial term
> sigma is the standard deviation for the non spatial term
>
> ONES is the identity matrix
> DELTA is a diagonal matrix, whose entries delta_ii = 1 /  the # of neighbors of row i
> H is a binary then row standardized adjacency matrix (eg each row sums to 1) where h_ij = ( b_ij / # of neighbors of row i) and b_ij = 1 if i is a neighbor of j; 0 otherwise.
>
> phi = 0.3 = 1 / max{ eigenvalue(-DELTA^(-1/2) * H * DELTA ^ (1/2) }
>
> I believe my model specification is correct and my data manipulations (via [R]) should be correct, but I question if my stan implementation is correct.
>
> Attachments
> For your consideration, I've attached 4 files:
>
> All of the necessary data to feed into stan
> fake_spatial_bym_stan.RData
>
> The two files that manipulated the data
> setup_stan_maf_data.R (and calls stan)
> setup_stan_maf_init.R
>
> The stan model file
> maf_convolution_model_sfstd.stan
>
> Specific Stan Model File
>
> data {
>     int<lower=0> N; // number of areas
>     matrix[N,N] H;  // area adjacency matrix row standardized (ea row sums to 1)
>     matrix[N,N] Delta;  // diagonal matrix in BYM 1991, sfstd model B1
>     matrix[N,N] Ones; // diag matrix of ones for identity
>     real phi; // phi = 1/maxeigval(Delta*H*Delta)
>     int<lower=0> O[N];  // observed cases
>     vector[N] E;  // expected cases
>     vector[N] x1;  // covariate
> }
>
> transformed data {
>   vector[N] zeros;  // zeros for mean of MVN specification
>   for (i in 1:N)
>         zeros[i] <- 0.0;
> }
>
> parameters {
>     real alpha0;  // intercept
>     real alpha1;  // coefficient on covariates
>
>     vector[N] beta1;  // random effect (CAR)
>     vector[N] beta2;  // random effect normal
>
>     real<lower=1e-5> prec_sre;  // precision of CAR
>     real<lower=1e-5> prec_nre;  // precision of normal
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
>     // turn precisions to variances
>     real sigma_sq;
>     real tau_sq;
>     sigma_sq <- 1.0 / (prec_nre * prec_nre);
>     tau_sq <- 1.0 / (prec_sre * prec_sre);
> }
>
> model {
>     matrix[N,N] Sigma_sre;  // covariance matrix for CAR
>     matrix[N,N] Sigma_nre;  // covariance matrix for normal RE
>     real beta1_mean;
>     vector[N] beta1_stz;  // centered spatial re
>     vector[N] log_mu;
>
>     prec_sre ~ gamma(1,1);    // precision of spatial re
>     prec_nre ~ gamma(0.5, 0.0005);    // precision of normal re
>
>     // spatial re
>     Sigma_sre <- (tau_sq * inverse(Ones - phi * H)) * Delta;
>     beta1 ~ multi_normal(zeros, Sigma_sre);
>     beta1_mean <- mean(beta1);
>     beta1_stz <- beta1 - beta1_mean;
>
>     // nonspatial re
>     Sigma_nre <- sigma_sq*Ones;
>     beta2 ~ multi_normal(zeros, Sigma_nre);
>
>     // fixed effects
>     // no explicit prior on alpha0 (implicit improper flat prior)
>     alpha1 ~ normal(0.0, sqrt(1e5));
>
>     // process model
>     log_mu <- log(E) + alpha0 + alpha1 * x1 + beta1_stz + beta2;
>
>     // data model
>     O ~ poisson_log(log_mu);
> }
>
>
>
>
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Explicitly modeling correlation properly?
messages.body_plain:
That is correct.

In these simple hierarchies, tau -> theta -> y, the centered and non-centered parameterizations
just shift around the correlations to either tau -> theta or theta -> y.  If you have lots of data then theta -> y is
highly constrained and we want to break that correlation by using a centered parameterization.  If you have little
data then tau -> theta is highly constrained and we want to break that correlation by using a non-centered
parameterization.  To get an intuition as to why these “break” the correlations see Figure 4.

Of course if you have more than the tree layers then there are many more possible parameterizations
and things become more challenging.

> > >> Not a big deal. The real credit should go to Lewandowski, Kurowicka, and Joe but Bob and I have long since given up on being able to spell all that (hence the LKJ).
> > >>
> > >> Anyway, the broader point here is that calculating a matrix decomposition of a parameterized matrix in Stan is expensive, in part because the number of operations depends on the cube of the number of rows and in part because Stan has to use its auto-diff mechanism to compute the derivatives (which involves a chain rule whose number of links also depends on the cube of the number of rows) with respect to each scalar parameter. So if you do something like
> > >>
> > >> cholesky_decompose( diag_matrix(scales) * correlation_matrix * diag_matrix(scales) )
> > >>
> > >> or
> > >>
> > >> cholesky decompose( variance * correlation matrix )
> > >>
> > >> the cholesky_decompose() function just sees a square matrix and does not recognize that these are equivalent to
> > >>
> > >> diag_matrix(scales) * cholesky_decompose(correlation_matrix)
> > >>
> > >> and
> > >>
> > >> sqrt(variance) * choleksy_decompose(correlation_matrix)
> > >>
> > >> respectively (although as Philippe pointed out, this particular trick only applies with a diagonal matrix or a scalar).
> > >>

The attachment constructs and L such that L * L' is a correlation matrix that is distributed LKJ with shape parameter eta. So, if you use that, then the above expressions are equivalent to
> > >>
> > >> diag_matrix(scales) * L
> > >>
> > >> and
> > >>
> > >> sqrt(variance) * L
> > >>
> > >> But wait, there's more! If something is getting a multivariate normal prior (or more generally anything in the elliptical distribution family), then you don't want to actually use of the multi_normal functions (ideally, those should only be used for likelihoods of data). You can make Pars a local or transformed parameter that is a function of the primitive parameter vector z via the multivariate Matt trick:
> > >>
> > >> z ~ normal(0,1);
> > >>
> > >> This way avoids having to solve a triangular system of equations inside one of the multi_normal functions. All that said, none of this makes much difference when dealing with a 2x2 covariance matrix, but it is much better when the dimension of the covariance matrix is large.

> And of course, to dwell on the negative, what computation
> is slow in Stan compared to R?  log_determinant?  And
> you're talking about doing this in the generated quantities block
> and not with parameters?

Yes, the log_determinant of the dense matrix was substantially slower in Stan than R. Last time I tried it in Stan was in December so maybe things have changed, but at that time the log determinant of a 2000x2000 matrix took on the order of 100x longer to compute in Stan than R.

I was computing it in the transformed data block, at 1000 samples of p (which is the only parameter that the log determinant varies by, and is constrained [0,1)). That way I only have to do it once (well, 1000 times, but just during initialization), and in the model block can then simply do a linear interpolation of the log determinant based on the value of parameter p.

Now to speed things up I have just computed those 1000 samples of the log determinant once in R and pass them to Stan as data.

It's hacky, but since the log determinant is such a tiny contributor to the overall log probability and takes so long to compute it seems to be a worthwhile compromise.

> And we definitely have sparse matrix operations fairly high up
> on our to-do list (which is still beyond the immediate future,
> I'm afraid).

That's exciting to hear!

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Hierarchical regression with a within-subjects factor
messages.body_plain:
On Apr 2, 2014, at 1:18 AM, Andrew Ellis <a.w....@gmail.com> wrote:

> I recently asked this question on Cross-validated, but I think I'll have more luck here, as it's probably too software-related:

We're very friendly.

> I have data from a psychophysical experiment, in which I tested S subjects in J=2 conditions (within-subjects design). I am trying to model each subject's probability of giving a (binary) response y as a function of a stimulus parameter x; a standard approach is to use the cumulative normal density function as a psychometric function, which means that I'm using a probit regression model.
>
> Each observation is modelled as a mixture of Bernoulli distributions: either the subject does as he/she is supposed to or has an attentional lapse with a certain probability and then has to guess:
>
> for (n in 1:N) {
>  y[n] ~ bernoulli((1-lapse[subj[n]]) * Phi(alpha[subj[n], cond[n]] +
>  beta[subj[n], cond[n]] * x[n]) +
>  lapse[subj[n]] * guess[subj[n]]);
>  }
>
> Intercepts and slopes are allowed to vary by condition nested within subject. My aim is to estimate group-level intercept and slope parameters for each condition.
>
> The problem I'm having is how to allow for the fact that alpha and beta are correlated, and, additionally, the parameters for each condition are correlated for each subject, i.e. if subject A has a high alpha in condition 1, then also in condition 2.

Can't you just build a hierarchical model of the various effects,
such as subject-level and conditional level?  The only thing to be
careful about is to not overparameterize with too many degrees of
freedom.

The details obviously depend on the particular problem and what the
scales of alpha and beta are, but basically it's just a probit
regression.  You can also use logit --- it's a bit more efficient in Stan
(those cumulative distribution functions are expensive) and should
provide near identical results.

This is easier to work with than trying to model the correlations directly.
Stan, at least, doesn't give you good ways to structure the covariance
matrix to model these effects directly in a correlation-based prior.

There are lots of examples in Gelman and Hill's multilevel regression book.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Bob.  It looks I have to do algebra myself - there is no magic.

One approach folks are using is to make likelihood -e+300 when the set of parameters is infeasible.  Can this be done in Stan? For example:
likelihood <- function (theta, time, y)
{
    prob <- dnorm (y - model (theta, time), mean = 0, sd = sigma) # to model y~normal(model,sigma)
    if (theta is feasible) {
        return (sum (prob))
    } else {
        return (-e+300)
    }
}
Linas

messages.body_plain:
It’s worth nothing that from a theoretical perspective such a constraint
indicates that model has broken down — you’re ignoring interactions
or saturation effects that would yield physically reasonable results.
Consequently just about everything you do is going to be a hack.

If you want to absolutely ensure that the sum of the tree exponentials
is positive then declare a transformed parameter

real<lower=0> sum = A exp () + B exp() + C exp()

When the RHS is negative a constraint violation will be raised and
the proposal immediately rejected but it’ll be up to you to ensure
that the posterior mass with sum < 0 isn’t too large.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Modeling (translating lmer model)
messages.body_plain:
We're actually looking right now into ways of using something
like lme4's language --- there are already prototype implementations.
But for now, you still have to do it by hand.

One thing to look at if you're learning is the ARM models (linked
from the top-level Stan GitHub Wiki and also from the mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org>
pages).  These have all sorts of examples of varying slope, varying
intercept hierarchical models, not all of which are directly expressible
in the R/S expression language.

I put comments on the particular model inline below.

On Apr 2, 2014, at 7:17 AM, Brady DeHart <brady...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello,
>
>  I am a graduate student trying to learn Bayesian statistics and use rstan in R. I do a lot of small sample-size research and view Bayesian statistics as an important tool to apply to small clusters. Unfortunately, no one in my department has any experience in Bayesian statistics which means I am kinda on my own. I would greatly appreciate any help anyone is willing to give in helping me prepare my rstan model. I will completely understand if my question is too remedial for the purpose of this forum but I thought I would give it a try. Let me start with my multilevel model and an explanation of the variables.
>
> lmer(y ~ x1 + x2 + x1*x2 + (1 + x1 + x2 | ID)
>
> Sample size = 6
>
> y = Continues dependent variable. Range of scores = 0 to 15.
> x1 = Time variable in terms of sessions. Range of scores = 1 to 30
> x2 = Experimental condition. Scores = 1, 2, or 3. Note that each subject has one data point per session and each session corresponds to an experimental condition. This conditions are administered randomly. Therefore, there is approximately 10 data points per condition per subject.
> ID = ID number that identifies subject
>
> So far here is what I have for my rstan model
>
>
> data {
>           int<lower=1,upper=6> [J];                  // ID
>           int<lower=0,upper=30> [N];               //All.Scores
>           int<lower=1,upper=J> ID[N];             // ID variable
>           vector[N] y;                                     // Outcome
>           vector[N] x1;                                  // Session
>           vector[N] x2;                                  // Condition
>        }
> transformed data {
>           vector[N] inter;                             // interaction term
>           inter  <-  x1.*x2;
>        }
>   parameters {
>           vector[J] a;                  //random intercept
>           vector[J] b;                  //random slope x1
>           vector[J] c;                  //random slope x2
>           vector[2] beta;
>           real mu_a;
>           real mu_b;
>           real mu_c;
>           real mu_beta;
>           real<lower=0, upper=100> sigma_a
>           real<lower=0, upper=100> sigma_b
>           real<lower=0, upper=100> sigma_c
>           real<lower=0,upper=100> sigma_y
>      }

This all looks great!  Except maybe too-wide priors on the sigma terms --- are you
really expecting those to be as high as 200?  If not, you should use more reasonable
priors.   This is more a modeling issue than a Stan issue, though very fat priors can
negatively impact inference speed if the fat prior leads to a very fat posterior.
This is especially a problem with small data cases.

>
> From here, I am at a bit of a loss. If I understand things correctly, I don't have group level variables, only individual predictors.

The a, b, and c are group-level because they're indexed by J.
But maybe I'm misunderstanding your comment.

I'm not sure how the beta and mu_beta connect.

> I have not found an example online with 2 random slopes and a random intercept in the model for me to follow. The prior distributions will be assumed to be normal. I am also not entirely sure what to set the parameters of the prior distributions to. I would be vary grateful to anyone willing to provide some guidance to a beginner. Thank you all!

The model's trivial given your clean description.  You can just
add the priors as with all the other examples.  Then the model

> y ~ x1 + x2 + x1*x2 + (1 + x1 + x2 | ID)

just becomes (assuming beta are your coefficients and you up the size to 3; you
could use a different variable and different prior)

for (n in 1:N)
 y[n] ~ normal(beta[1] * x1[n]
               + beta[2] * x2[n]
               + beta[3] * inter
               + a[ID[n]]
               + b[ID[n]] * x1[n]
               + c[ID[n]] * x2[n],
               sigma);

a ~ normal(mu_a, sigma_a);
b ~ normal(mu_b, sigma_b);
c ~ normal(mu_c, sigma_c);

But the problem with this formulation is that it's overparameterized.
b and c are more general parameters than beta[1] and beta[2].

When you get this working, you may want to scatterplot the posterior
a, b, and c and see if there's enough covariance to be worth modeling
with a more general covariance-based prior by putting a, b, and c into
a vector and giving them a multivariate normal prior.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
>From a more practical perspective, if you do this:

>>     if (theta is feasible) {
>>         return (sum (prob))
>>     } else {
>>         return (-e+300)
>>     }

then when theta's not feasible, you lose all connection to
any of the parameters --- you just return a constant.  This
breaks all the gradient information, and makes it very hard for
HMC to get back to where it should be.

Rejecting as Michael suggests is a better approach if you can't
formulate a constraint.

I take it that the A, B, and C being outside the exp() is
critical for some reason?

- Bob

On Apr 2, 2014, at 9:42 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> It’s worth nothing that from a theoretical perspective such a constraint
> indicates that model has broken down — you’re ignoring interactions
> or saturation effects that would yield physically reasonable results.
> Consequently just about everything you do is going to be a hack.
>
> If you want to absolutely ensure that the sum of the tree exponentials
> is positive then declare a transformed parameter
>
> real<lower=0> sum = A exp () + B exp() + C exp()
>
> When the RHS is negative a constraint violation will be raised and
> the proposal immediately rejected but it’ll be up to you to ensure
> that the posterior mass with sum < 0 isn’t too large.
>
> On Apr 2, 2014, at 1:28 AM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Thanks, Bob.  It looks I have to do algebra myself - there is no magic.
>>
>> One approach folks are using is to make likelihood -e+300 when the set of parameters is infeasible.  Can this be done in Stan? For example:
>> likelihood <- function (theta, time, y)
>> {
>>     prob <- dnorm (y - model (theta, time), mean = 0, sd = sigma) # to model y~normal(model,sigma)
>>     if (theta is feasible) {
>>         return (sum (prob))
>>     } else {
>>         return (-e+300)
>>     }
>> }
>>
>> Linas
>>
>> On 4/1/2014 7:04 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>> On Apr 1, 2014, at 8:28 PM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com>
>>>  wrote:
>>>
>>>
>>>> Thanks, Ben.  How to allow situations such as A,B>0 but C<0?  The plasma concentration profile may be represented as a sum of exponentials with positive and negative coefficients.
>>>>
>>> Unless you know something about the constraints on values,
>>> the bounds on C given A and B are data dependent.  You can
>>> just do the algebra, though:
>>>
>>>   0 < A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time) + C * exp(-k3 * time)
>>>
>>> iff
>>>
>>>   -[A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time)] < C * exp(-k3 * time)
>>>
>>> iff
>>>
>>>   -[A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time)] / exp(-k3 * time) < C
>>>
>>> So you need to take the lower bound for C to be
>>>
>>>   max_{k1,k2,k3,time}
>>>     -[A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time)]
>>>     / exp(-k3 * time)
>>>
>>> It may not actually be possible to calculate this in Stan, because
>>> you need the bound at the point you declare C, at least to support
>>> the direct constraint approach.
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>>> I think when I am done with this model I am willing to donate the model (standard 2-compartmental) along with anti-cancer drug data (documented in open literature) as an example of PK modeling in Stan.
>>>>
>>> Thanks.  That'd be great, and we'd of course provide
>>> attribution and proper credit!
>>>
>>> - Bob
>>>
>>>
>>>> Linas
>>>> On 4/1/2014 12:34 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>>>>
>>>>> In this case, I think you will be fine. Ultimately, you can use the lognormal density, so just do
>>>>>
>>>>> y ~ lognormal(log_model,sigma);
>>>>>
>>>>> but first you have to create the log_model array. In your case,
>>>>>
>>>>> A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time) + C * exp(-k3 * time)
>>>>> ==
>>>>> exp(log_A) * exp(-k1 * time) + exp(log_B) * exp(-k2 * time)+exp(log_C) * exp(-k3 * time)
>>>>> ==
>>>>> exp(log_A - k1 * time) + exp(log_B - k2 * time) + exp(log_C - k3 * time)
>>>>>
>>>>> Thus, log_model is in the form of a log_sum_exp() of a vector of length 3 (which also helps with the numerical stability of this thing):
>>>>>
>>>>> for(time in 1:8) {
>>>>>   vector[3] temp;
>>>>>   temp[1] <- log_A - k1 * time;
>>>>>   temp[2] <- log_B - k2 * time;
>>>>>   temp[3] <- log_C - k3 * time;
>>>>>   log_model[time] <- log_sum_exp(temp);
>>>>> }
>>>>> y ~ lognormal(log_model, sigma);
>>>>>
>>>>> You just need to declare log_A, log_B, and log_C as parameters rather than A, B, and C.
>>>>>
>>>>> Ben
>>>>>
>>>>> On Tuesday, April 1, 2014 12:17:21 PM UTC-4, Linas Mockus wrote:

>>>>>
>>>>> I meant A*exp(-k1*time)+B*exp(-k2*time)+C*exp(-k3*time) >=0.

messages.subject: Re: Please help..Basic Issue
messages.body_plain:
This looks like an issue with R's factor type. It stores an internal list of integer codes, and when you coerce it to numeric or integer, it just returns those codes. So to get the raw form back, you need an indirect route like:

x <- as.numeric( as.character( x.factor ) )

For CCG, looks like it is hexadecimal or such? So some conversion will be needed additionally, unless R is smart enough to recognize the base, which I doubt. And Pract has letters in it too, so some more manual processing is likely needed.

messages.body_snippet:
Hi all!

Suppose that I have the following multivariate model,

Y[n]=B*Y[n-1] +SIGMA*error

where Y is a vector. When estimating the dynamic model, I would like STAN to discard the draws of the matrix

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Discarding explosive draws in a multivariate time series model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Discarding explosive draws in a multivariate time series model
messages.body_plain:
We'd recommend (and I'm channeling Andrew here) just leaving
the variables unconstrained and seeing what the fit looks like.
Things won't work well in the sampler if the fit's up against
a constraint boundary anyway.

If you must constrain, you're probably better off thinking about
it the other way around --- start with valid eigenvalues and then build
up.  I'm not sure how easy that is, but rejection is not a great idea
in terms of sampling efficiency.

I'm not sure if just throwing out draws that violate the constraint
would lead to a valid sampler.

- Bob

On Apr 2, 2014, at 5:50 PM, Carlos <car...@montesgaldon.com> wrote:

> Hi all!
>
> Suppose that I have the following multivariate model,
>
> Y[n]=B*Y[n-1] +SIGMA*error
>
> where Y is a vector. When estimating the dynamic model, I would like STAN to discard the draws of the matrix B that are non stationary. That is, I will need to compute the eigenvalues and check that the modulus of all of them are inside the unit circle. The pseudocode would be,
>
> model{
>
>     EV    <-eigenvalues(B);
>
>     # Now I would need a piece of code that determines if the modulus of each eigenvalue is smaller than one. I guess there is nothing like if(all(abs(EV)<1)) then blah blah... but it is possible to do it creating an index and doing a loop. However, I also need to compute the modulus of the eigenvalues in case they are complex. Assume that if the index >= 1 then there is at least one eigenvalue outside the unit circle. Then, I can do
>

>    Y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(B*Y[(n-1)], SIGMA);

>    if_else(index>=1, increment_log_prob(negative_infinity(), increment_log_prob(multi_normal_cholesky_log(Y[n]-B*Y[(n-1)], SIGMA)));
>
> }
>
> I know that STAN can compute eigenvalues for symmetric matrices, but B is not necessarily symmetric. Cut, is it possible to use a routine from other C++ libraries to compute the eigenvalues and its modulus? If so, how could I do it? Any idea guess? Also, if I use other C++ libraries, can I still use RStan, or should I switch to the command line STAN version?
>
> Thank you!
>
> PS: Obviously, other option is to estimate the model without imposing the constraint, and then, once I recover the draws from the posterior distribution, I can discard the ones that lead to explosive systems. The advantage of this would be that if I have to discard a lot of them, that might be evidence against stationarity of the data... But I am not sure what is more efficient/correct in this case
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Well, yes, that would be a good idea too. I have a MATLAB code that builds stationary B for any amount of lags... The idea would be to generate the eigenvalues (with uniform[-1,1] priors, most likely), and then the eigenvectors with normal distributions. I don't know how efficient it would be or if the model would be identified, but I might give it a try :)

This is the MATLAB code that generates stable coefficients, and it would be more or less the same in STAN, I guess...

function [M] = generate_stable_coefficients(K,P)

% Parameters

% K=Number of endogenous variables
% P=Number of lags

% Generate eigenvalues. We need KxP eigenvalues.

evalue = unifrnd(-0.99,0.99,K*P,1); % Inside the unit circle and not big

% Generate eigenvectors. First, I will randomly generate the first K rows
% of the matrix V of eigenvectors

evector = zeros(K*P,K*P);

evector(1:K,:) = rand(K,K*P);

% Now, we have to complete the matrix of eigenvectors

k1 = K+1;
kp = K*P;

for kk= k1:kp

    for jj=1:kp

        evector(kk,jj) = evector(kk-K,jj)/evalue(jj,1);

    end

end

% Solve for matrix A

G = diag(evalue);

A = evector * G * inv(evector);

M = A(1:K,:); % Extract the coefficients A1, A2, A3...

transformed parameters {
  real A;
  real B;
  real C;
  real<lower=0> sum;

  A <- …;
  B <- …;
  C <- ..;

  sum <- A * exp(-k1 * time) + B * exp(-k2 * time) + C * exp(-k3 * time);

}

When the transformed parameters are computed an exception will be thrown if sum < 0
causing an immediate rejection even before the model block is executed.

> > Generating Eigenvectors is tricky --- we have the unit_length type,
> > but nothing to keep them orthogonal.

> > Maybe it'd be possible to rotate a bunch of orthogonal unit-length
> > vectors with a correlation matrix to get the right effect.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > On Apr 2, 2014, at 6:21 PM, Carlos <car...@montesgaldon.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Well, yes, that would be a good idea too. I have a MATLAB code that builds stationary B for any amount of lags... The idea would be to generate the eigenvalues (with uniform[-1,1] priors, most likely), and then the eigenvectors with normal distributions. I don't know how efficient it would be or if the model would be identified, but I might give it a try :)
> > >
> > > This is the MATLAB code that generates stable coefficients, and it would be more or less the same in STAN, I guess...
> > >
> > > function [M] = generate_stable_coefficients(K,P)
> > >
> > > % Parameters
> > >
> > > % K=Number of endogenous variables
> > > % P=Number of lags
> > >
> > > % Generate eigenvalues. We need KxP eigenvalues.
> > >
> > > evalue = unifrnd(-0.99,0.99,K*P,1); % Inside the unit circle and not big
> > >
> > > % Generate eigenvectors. First, I will randomly generate the first K rows
> > > % of the matrix V of eigenvectors
> > >
> > > evector = zeros(K*P,K*P);
> > >
> > > evector(1:K,:) = rand(K,K*P);
> > >
> > > % Now, we have to complete the matrix of eigenvectors
> > >
> > > k1 = K+1;
> > > kp = K*P;
> > >
> > > for kk= k1:kp
> > >
> > >     for jj=1:kp
> > >
> > >         evector(kk,jj) = evector(kk-K,jj)/evalue(jj,1);
> > >
> > >     end
> > >
> > > end
> > >
> > > % Solve for matrix A
> > >
> > > G = diag(evalue);
> > >
> > > A = evector * G * inv(evector);
> > >
> > > M = A(1:K,:); % Extract the coefficients A1, A2, A3...
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, April 2, 2014 12:07:58 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > We'd recommend (and I'm channeling Andrew here) just leaving
> > > the variables unconstrained and seeing what the fit looks like.
> > > Things won't work well in the sampler if the fit's up against
> > > a constraint boundary anyway.
> > >
> > > If you must constrain, you're probably better off thinking about
> > > it the other way around --- start with valid eigenvalues and then build
> > > up.  I'm not sure how easy that is, but rejection is not a great idea
> > > in terms of sampling efficiency.
> > >
> > > I'm not sure if just throwing out draws that violate the constraint
> > > would lead to a valid sampler.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > On Apr 2, 2014, at 5:50 PM, Carlos <car...@montesgaldon.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Hi all!
> > > >
> > > > Suppose that I have the following multivariate model,
> > > >
> > > > Y[n]=B*Y[n-1] +SIGMA*error
> > > >
> > > > where Y is a vector. When estimating the dynamic model, I would like STAN to discard the draws of the matrix B that are non stationary. That is, I will need to compute the eigenvalues and check that the modulus of all of them are inside the unit circle. The pseudocode would be,
> > > >
> > > > model{
> > > >
> > > >     EV    <-eigenvalues(B);
> > > >
> > > >     # Now I would need a piece of code that determines if the modulus of each eigenvalue is smaller than one. I guess there is nothing like if(all(abs(EV)<1)) then blah blah... but it is possible to do it creating an index and doing a loop. However, I also need to compute the modulus of the eigenvalues in case they are complex. Assume that if the index >= 1 then there is at least one eigenvalue outside the unit circle. Then, I can do
> > > >
> > > >    Y[n] ~ multi_normal_cholesky(B*Y[(n-1)], SIGMA);
> > > >    if_else(index>=1, increment_log_prob(negative_infinity(), increment_log_prob(multi_normal_cholesky_log(Y[n]-B*Y[(n-1)], SIGMA)));
> > > >
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > I know that STAN can compute eigenvalues for symmetric matrices, but B is not necessarily symmetric. Cut, is it possible to use a routine from other C++ libraries to compute the eigenvalues and its modulus? If so, how could I do it? Any idea guess? Also, if I use other C++ libraries, can I still use RStan, or should I switch to the command line STAN version?

messages.body_plain:
Then from where are the unsatisfied constrains coming?  If you have a self-consistent system
then the solutions should satisfy all of the necessary constraints tautologically and the only
issue would be one of parameterization.  Per this definition a system of ODEs that doesn’t
satisfy all of the constraints is an approximation, even if it has a closed-form solution.

As we have discussed, limiting the parameter space to where the approximate model is valid
can be feasible provided that the space of valid parameters is relatively well-behaved.  The
more constraints you add, however, are going to make the model harder and harder to
specify, let alone fit.

Were I Andrew I’d invoke the Folk Theorem, http://andrewgelman.com/2009/05/24/handy_statistic/.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I know this is an old thread, but I am facing a problem where using a data augmentation could in theory improve my MCMC. Because in my model (depending on the prior) I would have very nice full conditional distributions which I could sample directly from, whereas without the data augmentation step I must sample from proposals instead.

Anyway, my code seems to work nicely in stan without the data augmentation step, but I am puzzled with the sentece in the email "this part is executed via data augmentation, which is obviously impossible in Stan.". I wonder why it is obviously? Could someone give me a hint why is that? I tried to do the data augmentation in stan and I failed, mainly because I would have an integer parameter and that was the problem. Is that the reason? Or is there something else that explains why data augmentation cannot be done in stan.

Cheers,
Leo Bastos

Michael,

Model is good as long as parameters are feasible.  For example if we take a bathtub and parameters are water rates entering and leaving the bathtub and the rate of leaving bathtub is higher than the rate entering bathtub then bathtub will get dry even if it was full initially.  Assuming constant parameters solution of ODE which describes this process will eventually lead to a negative level.  This is in essence 1-compartmental model.  2-compartmental model is a bit trickier.  So assumption  that rate parameters are constant is wrong.  Therefore we end up with enforcing constraint that the level in bathtub (or plasma concentration) > 0. Kind of hack... I am looking for an elegant solution - perhaps it exists, I don't know. This should be more general than PK modeling.
Linas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] adding constraints for parameters in Stan model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] adding constraints for parameters in Stan model
messages.body_plain:
Right, this is what I was saying.  You have a model that is not consistent with the physical system outside a certain neighborhood
of parameter space.  Within that neighborhood fits are okay, but if the data pushes you outside of that neighborhood then (a) you
have strong evidence that the model validity has broken down an (b) your fitting will start to perform poorly.

Now you can ignore the conflict between the data and the model validity (not recommended, of course) and try to force inference
within the valid neighborhood, but this will only work okay in practice if the valid neighborhood is relatively well-behaved.  For example,
if a single parameter is constrained to be in a sweet spot then it's easy enough to constrain that one parameter and not limit performance
much.

But the constraints you have discussed are not simple.  The positivity constraint induces highly non-linear constraints in the parameter
space, and introducing singular k1 != k2 constraints will induce further pathologies.

Yes, you can hack all of this stuff into a Stan model but the resulting posterior is going to become ugly, and performance is going to suffer
dramatically and this is why I am recommending against it.  It's the Folk Theorem all over again.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Help with the structure of a multilevel model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Help with the structure of a multilevel model
messages.body_plain:
In Stan, you need to declare variables with constraints
that match their support in the model.  So if you're
going to have a uniform(0,1000) distribution for a parameter,
it needs to be declared lower=0,upper=1000.  And in general,
we'd recommend realistic scales on the priors rather than
very fat priors like uniform(0,1000) [unless that's the scale of
your data].

I'm afraid I didn't quite understand what you were trying to do from
your description.

I find it easiest to think about modeling in terms of a process
to generate the data from the parameters (and size constants and
fixed hyperparameters).  The model you're proposing doesn't fit this
generative model because you sample the data variable y twice.  But
then you're really fitting two distinct models, because the second
sampling statement for y seems unrelated to the first.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Mixture modelling and multiple modes.
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Mixture modelling and multiple modes.
messages.body_plain:
I discuss this problem a bit in the mixture modeling chapter
and in the problematic posteriors chapter.

The biggest problem is that forcing mu[0] < mu[1], you can still swap
indices if the posterior means of the two mixture components are near each
other (on their scales).

Also, forcing this relationship means that you can't do inference
about how well separated the means are, for instance, Pr[mu[0] < mu[1]] = 1.
I'm pretty sure it will also affect the correlation of mu[0] and mu[1] in the
posterior.  Basically, it's not just the same model with identity resolved.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean,

Thanks for asking. I'm responding below:

On Fri, Apr 4, 2014 at 1:05 AM, Sean O'Riordain <seor...@tcd.ie> wrote:

> Good moorning Stan Developers!
>
> My problem involves thousands of integers with 20+ possible values so I understand that I cannot sum across them so easily.

That shouldn't be too difficult if you do it programmatically. Take a look at the normal mixture model with K components for reference:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/models/basic_estimators/normal_mixture_k.stan

You should be able to put the "thousands of integers" in a single loop and the "20+ possible values" in a second loop and sum them out with any issues, unless I'm missing something fundamental (which may very well be the case).

> I understand that there can be no gradient for integer sampling so HMC won't work in the same way.
>
> Could you indicate the time scale for when Stan will be able to sample integers please?

It's not on our immediate list of things to do, so it probably will not be done in 2014. If anyone is really keen on it, we're happy to take implementations from people. We've thrown around the idea of slice sampling across the discrete parameters and using NUTS for the continuous parameters, but honestly, we don't have the time to do everything we want.

While we're on the topic, here are some of the things we're working on and very, very rough timeline:

2014
-------
L-BFGS for optimization
functions as part of the Stan language
refactoring of Stan so it'll be easy to write a wrapper in any system
JSON data interface
max marginal likelihood
+ making Stan faster, adding more distributions, killing bugs, and extensions to each of the existing interfaces

2014+
-------
Variational Bayes
Expectation Propagation
replacement of auto-diff library
Riemann Manifold HMC
differential equations as part of the Stan language

We've got our hands full at this point, but I wouldn't say it can't be done in the near future. It's just not on the development team's short list of things to do. Each of us has some research interest at heart and we currently don't have a champion for discrete parameters. If someone wants to implement it, we are very happy to get it incorporated.

Hopefully that answers your question and doesn't discourage you from using Stan. We (the development team) are all lurking on this list, so feel free to reach out with additional questions.

messages.body_plain:
To reinforce what Daniel said, loops and arithmetic are fast, so
summing across 20 possible values for thousands of items may not be
as bad as you think.

When you have to sample a discrete variable form its conditional,
you wind up having to do pretty much the same arithmetic anyway.

There's a huge advantage to marginalizing in that the sampler itself
becomes much more efficient --- it's the Rao-Blackwell theorem in
action.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling integers
messages.body_plain:
What's the form of the summation in the model?

The case we can't figure out how to deal with is something
like a zero-inflated normal that gives probability mass to
a value of exactly 0 and interpolates that with a normal.  If
we use those as regression predictors, the sums are intractable
because we need to consider all the interactions.  If we had 10,000
coefficients, that'd mean a 10000-summation, with the inside being
a regression for a single sparseness pattern among the 2^(10000).

So if that's what you're dealing with, there's not much hope of
doing it in Stan.  It may also be seriously multi-modal and difficult
to explore with any software, even if it has discrete sampling.

Something like a latent discrete parameter that's attached to
data items is much easier to deal with.

- Bob

Autodiff vectors and matrices (and arrays) are just collections
of autodiff scalars.  So what's going on in the code below
is that x_return is a matrix and its entries are getting populated
with gradients.  If you need richer gradients, you need to replace
precomp_v_vari.  In general, you can just use Stan operations and
they produce the right output and gradients --- you only need to
worry about something more complicated if you want to partially
evaluate (i.e., unfold) the derivative calcs.

If you really want examples of how to do that efficiently, look
at some .hpp files in stan/agrad/rev/matrix/.

On the good news front, I've finished writing functions, and will
write a general ODE solver that encapsulates all of this behind the
scenes based on the system function.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sampling integers
messages.body_plain:
Adding discrete sampling would require a substantial amount of
work to

 * deal with the discrete parameter data structures.

 * change the constraints in the parser and assumptions
   in the code generator

 * figure out some adaptation scheme

 * do the sampling itself, which would have to be alternated with
   HMC, NUTS, etc. --- ideally this would be a general refactor to
   allow arbitrary block sampling

All of this is doable by us.  The real roadblock is that there is
no good way to get the conditional posterior of the discrete parameters.
In BUGS/JAGS, you could find the Markov blanket because the model
was structured as a directed acyclic graph syntactically.

The problem with gluing from the outside is that you'd have to
startup Stan again each time with the new discrete parameter values as
data.  That would undercut all of our adaptation.  But then we're not
exactly sure how discrete sampling would interact with our continuous
adaptation, either.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm trying to speedup fitting a Poisson regression using stan. I'd like to have the time require to fit model in stan comparable to fitting it using glm in R. I have a dataset that has 7875 observations and 9 parameters to estimate. I'm using doMC to run parallel chains as follows:

options(cores=4) #set this appropriate to your system
    registerDoMC()
    num_chains <- 4
    fun <- function(){
          fit <- stan(file='Desktop/HiC.stan',data = HiC_data,iter = 1000,chains = 1, verbose = FALSE)
          return(fit)
    }

    #parallel case
    stime <- system.time({
    parallel_fit <- foreach(i = 1:num_chains) %dopar% fun()
        })[3]/60
    show(sprintf("Time in min to fit the model %f",stime))
    fit <- sflist2stanfit(parallel_fit)

In terms of processing time, parallel stan took 43 minutes and glm in R to  0.016850 minutes. Any suggestions?

Best,
Mark

> All of this is doable by us.  The real roadblock is that there is

For the last month, I've thought to myself that the path of least resistance was to use a "universal" PRNG such as

http://statmath.wu.ac.at/unuran/

which also has an R interface for reference

http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/Runuran/

The unuran library is GPL, so we can't build it into libstan, but there is nothing technically illegal if stanc generates a .cpp file that links against it and generates code that uses it. So, basically once the leapfrogger stops on the proposal for the continuous parameters, we would just need to follow this example in the docs

http://statmath.wu.ac.at/unuran/doc/unuran.html#Example_005f2

that basically wraps a call to the log-posterior in doubles / ints and draw the discrete parameters one at a time conditional on the continuous parameters.

Still not trivial.

Ben

On Tuesday, April 8, 2014 2:13:01 PM UTC-4, Mark Carty wrote:
> In terms of processing time, parallel stan took 43 minutes and glm in R to  0.016850 minutes. Any suggestions?

Hard to say without seeing the .stan file. But

Don't recompile the model on each core. Compile it once at the start and call stan() with the fit argument
Use y ~ poisson_log(log_lambda) rather than y ~ poisson(lambda)
Don't do y[i] ~ poisson(lambda[i])
Don't compare MCMC wall time to ML wall time. A better comparison would be to use the optimizing() function in rstan to get the ML estimates or the MAP estimates, in which case Stan might even be faster but it is not as convenient as summary.glm() is to get standard errors and confidence intervals and stuff. Andrew is working on some stuff to automate drawing from the sampling distribution.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Reflection invariance
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for this. I got it implemented and played with it, and have a system that’s working well.

In the end, I took a different direction, which I’ll report here for the benefit of anyone else struggling with a comparable situation.

The problem I kept having, even using solutions like the one below, is that the gammas kept getting pushed toward zero (and if I allowed sigma_gamma to vary, /it/ got pushed toward zero). In the end, I realized that it was because I had a bimodal distribution, with one mode on the negative side for the reverse-coded items, and another on the positive side for the others. That caused all the problems one would expect. So I changed tack, reverse-coding the items I knew ought to be reverse-coded, and estimated

gamma ~ normal(mu_gamma,sigma_gamma);

I obliged the hyperprior mu_gamma to be > sigma_gamma/2, to keep it away from zero and ensure that most of the density of the parameters would be positive, and gave it a prior of cauchy(1,5). There’s no restriction on gamma itself, but those constraints on the priors and hyperpriors ensured that there was very little density on the negative side of any of the gammas estimated.

If I didn’t have prior knowledge that would let me reverse-code items, I’d probably have to do some sort of mixture model, I guess, or use a extremely diffuse (or uniform) prior on gamma and orient it as Bob suggested.

Thanks,
Josh

On Mar 24, 2014, at 8:03 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> It helps if you send more of the Stan code.
>
> I'm guessing the problem you're having is with constraints.
> Parameters need to be declared with constraints that match
> their support.  Stan's limited constraint language makes it
> hard to do what Andrew was suggesting in ARM (if I understand
> corectly), namely constraining one element of an array to
> be positive and one negative.
>
> The natural solution in Stan is this:
>
> parameters {
>  real<lower=0> gamma_pos;
>  real<upper=0> gamma_neg;
>  vector[K-2] gamma_rest;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>  vector[K] gamma;
>  gamma[1] <- gamma_pos;
>  gamma[2] <- gamma_neg;
>  for (k in 3:K)
>    gamma[k] <- gamma_rest[k-2];
> }
> model {
>  gamma_pos ~ normal(0,1);
>  gamma_neg ~ normal(0,1);
>  gamma_rest ~ normal(0,1);
>
> You don't need the truncations as they're built into
> the constraints (though you would need them and the model
> would need to be made more complex.  All the above would
> be more efficient as just:
>
>  gamma ~ normal(0,1);
>
> Sorry it's so clunky --- it's only to deal with the varying constraints.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Mar 24, 2014, at 8:48 AM, Joshua Rosenau <josh.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> For an ideal point model (for simplicity, call it IRT) I'm working on, I'd like to let discrimination be positive or negative, since unpooled analyses I've run show that some discriminations do seem to take on different signs in different countries, and I don't want to assume that my reverse coding will always be right.
>>
>> In ARM, it's recommended to add a predictor x coding one person (or item) as positive, the other negative, the rest 0, and estimate an orienting parameter d such that discrimination[i] = x[i]*d+eta[i].
>>
>> I gave this approach a shot in Stan (checking it against the implementation in the ARM example posted at github), and the models are failing to converge after long, long runs, and often not even generating estimated discriminations of opposite signs for the items chosen! (I chose those items both because of prior knowledge about the nature of the items and because a standard IRT analysis using ltm shows them to be the items with the most positive and negative discriminations, respectively).
>>
>> I've also experimented with constraining the priors, using a loop in the model section specifying:
>>
>> for (i in 1:K){
>>   if (x[i] == 1) gamma[i] ~ normal(0,1)T[0,];
>>   else if (x[i] == -1) gamma[i] ~ normal(0,1)T[,0];
>>   else gamma[i] ~ normal(0,1);
>> }
>>
>> It converges more quickly, but gives me results that don't make sense (i.e., other questions that I know should have large, negative discriminations are estimated with large, positive discriminations).
>>
>> When I reverse-code the items and give gamma a log-normal prior, the results match my expectations based on the ltm analysis, which makes me confident that the rest of the model is fine.
>>
>> Can anyone offer suggestions of other ways to address reflection invariance in Stan? Or a different way that I might think about this problem that would obviate the issue?
>>
>> Thanks,
>> Josh

messages.body_plain:
We've had problems with memory leaks for softmax(categorical(...))
before, but I thought we'd solved them.  Time to take another
look.  Which version of RStan are you using?

The distribution you should be using anyway is categorical_logit,
with

  categorial_logit(alpha) =def= categorical(softmax(alpha))

In terms of mixing, there are additive invariance issues with using
K unconstrained parameters for a K-simplex;  see the manual chapter
on problematic posteriors;  here that's reflected in your d
and alpha parameters, which you can see have very wide posteriors
for the model as formulated.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Stan's licensure
messages.body_plain:
All of the core Stan C++ is BSD, as is CmdStan.  We'll make
that clearer soon --- we're about to refactor CmdStan out
of the core Stan C++.  We've kept the core C++ clean in terms
of dependencies in part os that we could maintain BSD.

We could have factored RStan into a BSD part and a GPL part,
but it seemed like too much work, since the resulting BSD code
would pretty much by definition only be usable by the rest of
RStan --- everything else is getting pulled into the Stan C++
aPI core.  Almost everything in the R world is GPL-ed, so it
doesn't seem like such a burden there.

PyStan is GPL-ed, but that could be loosened if Allen were
amenable --- we left the copyright up to him.  Python's license
is very open and NumPy is new BSD (i.e., 3-clause).

I'd rather not sign away rights without reading them --- so
I'd say no to "AND ANY LATER versions" on general principle.

- Bob

On Apr 8, 2014, at 9:35 PM, Avraham Adler <avraha...@gmail.com> wrote:

> 	• Is there a reason that RStan and PyStan are not multi-licensed under the BSD3 as well to allow for more permissive use? By licensing CmdStan under the BSD3, the owners indicate that they aren't firm copyleftists :)
> 	• Similarly, why not LGPL for R/PyStan?
> 	• May I suggest that even if licensing under the GPL alone that it should be GPLv3 AND ANY LATER versions, which would save major headaches if GPL ever comes out with a v4. The headache of GPL2 to 3 remains rather large.
> Thanks,
>
>
> Avi

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Reflection invariance
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for following up with a report.

These ideal-point-like models are especially tricky for parameterization.
I was using one for movie reviewer modeling and it had the same sort of problems,
some of which I may have falsely attributed to working in two dimensions.

- Bob

On Apr 9, 2014, at 2:12 AM, Joshua Rosenau <josh.r...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks for this. I got it implemented and played with it, and have a system that's working well.
>
> In the end, I took a different direction, which I'll report here for the benefit of anyone else struggling with a comparable situation.
>
> The problem I kept having, even using solutions like the one below, is that the gammas kept getting pushed toward zero (and if I allowed sigma_gamma to vary, /it/ got pushed toward zero). In the end, I realized that it was because I had a bimodal distribution, with one mode on the negative side for the reverse-coded items, and another on the positive side for the others. That caused all the problems one would expect. So I changed tack, reverse-coding the items I knew ought to be reverse-coded, and estimated
>
> gamma ~ normal(mu_gamma,sigma_gamma);
>
> I obliged the hyperprior mu_gamma to be > sigma_gamma/2, to keep it away from zero and ensure that most of the density of the parameters would be positive, and gave it a prior of cauchy(1,5). There's no restriction on gamma itself, but those constraints on the priors and hyperpriors ensured that there was very little density on the negative side of any of the gammas estimated.
>
> If I didn't have prior knowledge that would let me reverse-code items, I'd probably have to do some sort of mixture model, I guess, or use a extremely diffuse (or uniform) prior on gamma and orient it as Bob suggested.
>
> Thanks,
> Josh
>
> On Mar 24, 2014, at 8:03 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> It helps if you send more of the Stan code.
>>
>> I'm guessing the problem you're having is with constraints.
>> Parameters need to be declared with constraints that match
>> their support.  Stan's limited constraint language makes it
>> hard to do what Andrew was suggesting in ARM (if I understand
>> corectly), namely constraining one element of an array to
>> be positive and one negative.
>>
>> The natural solution in Stan is this:
>>
>> parameters {
>> real<lower=0> gamma_pos;
>> real<upper=0> gamma_neg;
>> vector[K-2] gamma_rest;
>> }
>> transformed parameters {
>> vector[K] gamma;
>> gamma[1] <- gamma_pos;
>> gamma[2] <- gamma_neg;
>> for (k in 3:K)
>>   gamma[k] <- gamma_rest[k-2];
>> }
>> model {
>> gamma_pos ~ normal(0,1);
>> gamma_neg ~ normal(0,1);
>> gamma_rest ~ normal(0,1);
>>
>> You don't need the truncations as they're built into
>> the constraints (though you would need them and the model
>> would need to be made more complex.  All the above would
>> be more efficient as just:
>>
>> gamma ~ normal(0,1);
>>
>> Sorry it's so clunky --- it's only to deal with the varying constraints.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>> On Mar 24, 2014, at 8:48 AM, Joshua Rosenau <josh.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>> For an ideal point model (for simplicity, call it IRT) I'm working on, I'd like to let discrimination be positive or negative, since unpooled analyses I've run show that some discriminations do seem to take on different signs in different countries, and I don't want to assume that my reverse coding will always be right.
>>>
>>> In ARM, it's recommended to add a predictor x coding one person (or item) as positive, the other negative, the rest 0, and estimate an orienting parameter d such that discrimination[i] = x[i]*d+eta[i].
>>>
>>> I gave this approach a shot in Stan (checking it against the implementation in the ARM example posted at github), and the models are failing to converge after long, long runs, and often not even generating estimated discriminations of opposite signs for the items chosen! (I chose those items both because of prior knowledge about the nature of the items and because a standard IRT analysis using ltm shows them to be the items with the most positive and negative discriminations, respectively).
>>>
>>> I've also experimented with constraining the priors, using a loop in the model section specifying:
>>>
>>> for (i in 1:K){
>>>  if (x[i] == 1) gamma[i] ~ normal(0,1)T[0,];
>>>  else if (x[i] == -1) gamma[i] ~ normal(0,1)T[,0];
>>>  else gamma[i] ~ normal(0,1);
>>> }
>>>
>>> It converges more quickly, but gives me results that don't make sense (i.e., other questions that I know should have large, negative discriminations are estimated with large, positive discriminations).
>>>
>>> When I reverse-code the items and give gamma a log-normal prior, the results match my expectations based on the ltm analysis, which makes me confident that the rest of the model is fine.
>>>
>>> Can anyone offer suggestions of other ways to address reflection invariance in Stan? Or a different way that I might think about this problem that would obviate the issue?
>>>
>>> Thanks,
>>> Josh
>>>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Help with the structure of a multilevel model
messages.body_plain:
There's a chapter on measurement error models in the manual.

Measurement error for Y usually gets rolled into the overall noise
term.  Measurement error for X is usually dealt with by assuming
a latent true value with measurement noise around it leading to the
observation.  And that's exactly how it gets coded in Stan.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Speeding up stan for big data!
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Speeding up stan for big data!
messages.body_plain:
The other issue is to decide how many samples you want and how long
it's taking to converge vs. sample.

1.  Check out the traceplots to measure how long
convergence actually takes --- we usually waste a lot of time here
on simple models allocating half the overall iterations to adaptation
(the reason it's set that way is because it's better for harder models).

2.  Decide how much error you want in the posterior estimates or other
quantities of interest.  One doesn't usually need more than 20 or 50
effective samples for most inferences.

Also, we don't want to say that MCMC is the right tool for every
problem.  If you only need an MLE and it can be expressed in the
language of glm(), by all means use glm!  As Ben says, we're working
on rolling out a full suite of point estimation tools for Stan --- they
should see release in the next six to twelve months.

- Bob

On Apr 8, 2014, at 8:27 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Tuesday, April 8, 2014 2:13:01 PM UTC-4, Mark Carty wrote:
> In terms of processing time, parallel stan took 43 minutes and glm in R to  0.016850 minutes. Any suggestions?
>
> Hard to say without seeing the .stan file. But
>
> 	• Don't recompile the model on each core. Compile it once at the start and call stan() with the fit argument
> 	• Use y ~ poisson_log(log_lambda) rather than y ~ poisson(lambda)
> 	• Don't do y[i] ~ poisson(lambda[i])
> 	• Don't compare MCMC wall time to ML wall time. A better comparison would be to use the optimizing() function in rstan to get the ML estimates or the MAP estimates, in which case Stan might even be faster but it is not as convenient as summary.glm() is to get standard errors and confidence intervals and stuff. Andrew is working on some stuff to automate drawing from the sampling distribution.
> Ben
>
>
>
>

Hi folks,

I finally got around to making use of the von_mises distribution that was added recently, and I was able to code up a working example of a hierarchical mixture (uniform+von_mises) model for circular data:

https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/10298188

However, I'm finding it slow to evaluate, yielding only 1000-2000 effective samples after a day of crunching on a relatively fast machine. While this is ok for now, I was hoping on increasing the complexity to the model, including adding parameters to evaluate correlations across levels of my random effect amongst the existing parameters. Any advice on tweaks I might apply to make the code more efficient?

Oh, and in case this is related, I'm getting really strong autocorrelation in the samples for most of the parameters, even with chains of length 1e5. There's also pretty strong crosscorrelation between a few pairs of parameters.

Thoughts?

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University
