messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, April 9, 2014 3:07:42 PM UTC-4, Ken Arnold wrote:
> I'm experimenting with modeling correlation / covariance matrices with LKJ priors and it seems like a cool approach. But I'm encountering trouble when I try to scale up to higher dimensionality. In particular, even if I could get the model to run, the K-choose-2 factors will be increasingly hard to estimate as K gets large.

This is something of a misconception. Yes, there are nominally K-choose-2 correlations to estimate but the volume of the sample space of K-dimensional correlation matrices shrinks for K > 6. In R, this is what you have to multiply by to get the density to integrate to 1

constant <- function(K, eta = 1) {
  if(K == 1) return(1)
  k <- 1:(K-1)
  log_constant <- -sum(k) / 2 * log(pi) + (K - 1) * lgamma(eta + (K-1)/2) -
    sum(lgamma(eta + (K-k-1)/2))
  return(exp(log_constant))
}
plot(sapply(1:43, constant), type = "l", log = "y", las = 1,
     xlab = "K", ylab = "Constant")

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-jvYG6wtPGDk/U0Web-lVZ0I/AAAAAAAAAOo/P5slF88MkiM/s1600/Rplot.png>

> One approach I was thinking of is using a low-rank approximation, perhaps a truncated Cholesky decomposition. Has anyone tried this? What might be a good way to implement it in Stan?

Short-rank correatlion matrices is one approach, but the first thing to try is the attachment, which generates the Cholesky factor, L, of a correlation matrix such that L * L' has a LKJ(eta) distribution. This will be much faster and avoid the numerical positive definiteness violations that you see.

Making that Cholesky factor have more rows than columns is not terribly difficult but the distribution of the implied correlation matrix is not LKJ anymore. You would get larger correlations than under the LKJ prior with eta = 1, when typically you prefer smaller correlations (which can be accomplished under the LKJ prior by making eta > 1). Also, the order in which you input the variables may matter. So, there is not a lot of analytical work for that case yet, and I doubt it is necessary very often. With K = 5000, the attachment does

 method = sample (Default)
   sample
     num_samples = 1000 (Default)
     num_warmup = 1000 (Default)
     save_warmup = 0 (Default)
     thin = 1 (Default)
     adapt
       engaged = 1 (Default)
       gamma = 0.050000000000000003 (Default)
       delta = 0.80000000000000004 (Default)
       kappa = 0.75 (Default)
       t0 = 10 (Default)
       init_buffer = 75 (Default)
       term_buffer = 50 (Default)
       window = 25 (Default)
     algorithm = hmc (Default)
       hmc
         engine = nuts (Default)
           nuts
             max_depth = 10 (Default)
         metric = diag_e (Default)
         stepsize = 1 (Default)
         stepsize_jitter = 0 (Default)
 id = 0 (Default)

   file = /tmp/onion.data.R
 init = 2 (Default)
 random
   seed = 4294967295 (Default)
 output
   file = output.csv (Default)
   diagnostic_file =  (Default)
   refresh = 100 (Default)

Gradient evaluation took 1.63379 seconds
1000 transitions using 10 leapfrog steps per transition would take 16337.9 seconds.
Adjust your expectations accordingly!

On Wed, Apr 9, 2014 at 2:12 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi folks,

> I finally got around to making use of the von_mises distribution that was added recently, and I was able to code up a working example of a hierarchical mixture (uniform+von_mises) model for circular data:
>
> https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/10298188
>
> However, I'm finding it slow to evaluate, yielding only 1000-2000 effective samples after a day of crunching on a relatively fast machine. While this is ok for now, I was hoping on increasing the complexity to the model, including adding parameters to evaluate correlations across levels of my random effect amongst the existing parameters. Any advice on tweaks I might apply to make the code more efficient?
>
> Oh, and in case this is related, I'm getting really strong autocorrelation in the samples for most of the parameters, even with chains of length 1e5. There's also pretty strong crosscorrelation between a few pairs of parameters.
>
> Thoughts?

Well, for one you can vectorize things a bit more.  Instead of:

//define sampling of unit-specific parameters
for (n in 1:N){
logitRho[n] ~ normal(logitRhoMean,logitRhoSD);
logKappa[n] ~ normal(logKappaMean,logKappaSD);
logitRhoEffect[n] ~ normal(logitRhoEffectMean,logitRhoEffectSD);
logKappaEffect[n] ~ normal(logKappaEffectMean,logKappaEffectSD);
}

just do

logitRho ~ normal(logitRhoMean,logitRhoSD);
logKappa ~ normal(logKappaMean,logKappaSD);
logitRhoEffect ~ normal(logitRhoEffectMean,logitRhoEffectSD);
logKappaEffect ~ normal(logKappaEffectMean,logKappaEffectSD);

This will help a little, depending on how large N is.

Also, you should be able to compute log(rho[]) directly from logitRho.

Finally, if 2*N << L, then it might be worth precomputing values and just indexing them when looping over L.

Those things should help speed up the model, but won't necessarily help with convergence issues and strong autocorrelations.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: P-value inflation problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan users

I’ve been using a Poisson regression to model the noise in count data arising from a next generation sequencing technique. I’m trying to identify events more extreme than the background (noise). I’ve been using a Poisson p-value to identify such events. I have a plot of log2 fold change of the observed count divided predicted count verses predicted count. From the plot, I have a p-value inflation problem. Too many events with a low Poisson mean are being called statistically significant at 1% FDR threshold. I do believe the Poisson regression is a good model for this data. I’ve done ten-fold cross-validation to evaluate the model’s performance on held-out data, and I do get a median Spearman correlation of 85%. I wanted to try the Bayesian posterior predictive p-value. That is, to generate yrep[i] ~ poisson(lambda[i]), and then calculate b.pvalue[i] ~ step(yrep[i] – y[i]) – 0.5*ifelse(yrep[i]-y[i]==0,1,0). My assumption is that posterior predictive p-value might be more stringent frequentist p-value. Does anyone give some advice on this problem?

Best,

Mark

Regarding the efficiency of the "Matt trick," Michael Betancourt noted in this group <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/dFFTF0n6mYo/lTIfqVN8AB8J> and in his paper <http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906>, that using centered parameters is effective when there is a lot of data vis-a-vis the parameters. In that case, shifting (some of) the correlation to the hyperparameters can be very useful. However, when there is only a little data, it may be more efficient use the non-centered versions (no Matt trick). He pointed us to Figure 8 in his paper if that helps.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: P-value inflation problem
messages.body_plain:
I can't really address your stats question, but once
you have lambda[i], can't you just generate the expectation
rather than sampling?  It'd be more efficient inferentially.

And in Stan, instead of

  step(yrep[i] - y[i])

you can just write

  (yrep[i] > y[i])

which takes on value 1 if condition is true and 0 otherwise.

Similarly,

  ifelse(yrep[i] - y[i] == 0, 1, 0)

can be replaced by just

  (yrep[i] == y[i])

which is 1 if they're equal and 0 otherwise.  That is, the conditions
act like they have indicator functions wrapped around them arithmetically.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Ok, I actually just realized that my idea probably wouldn't work as well as I'd thought but here it is.

In transformed data:

real neglog2pi;
neglog2pi <- -log(2.0 * pi());

and in transformed parameters:

vector[N] logrho[2];
vector[N] log1mrho_neglog2pi[2];

for (n in 1:N) {

  // compute rho and kappa here then...
  logrho[n,1] <- log(rho[n,1]);
  logrho[n,2] <- log(rho[n,2]);
  log1mrho_neglog2pi[n,1] <- log1m(rho[n,1]) + neglog2pi;
  log1mrho_neglog2pi[n,2] <- log1m(rho[n,2]) + neglog2pi;
}

then in model:

ps[1] <- logrho[unit[i],conditions[i]] + ...

ps[2] <- log1mrho_neglog2pi[unit[i],condition[i]];

This should shave some more time off so long as 2*N << L.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Apr 14, 2014, at 5:45 AM, Kazem <nasser...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks Bob for your valuable help.
> I have already fitted a mixture model with 4 latent classes. It works well!!!
> The syntax for a simple model without random effects in the model are as below:
> Now I have some more questions: (Please look at below)
>
> ########## Stan syntax
> data {
>   int k ;                           // Number of latent class
>   int ntot ;	    // Number of Observations
>   real Age[ntot] ;
>   int n ;                          // Number of individuals
>   int<lower=1> offset[51];
>   real <lower=0,upper=1> Season[ntot] ;
>   real <lower=0> TSPD[ntot] ;
>   real Hb[ntot];
>  }
>
> parameters {
>
>   simplex[k] pi[n];	//mixing proportions
>
>   real<lower=0,upper=1> sigma; //scale parameters of mixture components
>
>   vector[k] theta1;	         // Non-shared parameter
>
>   vector[3] beta;	 // Shared parameters
> }
>
> model {
>   real psi[k];
>   beta~normal(0,1);
>   theta1~normal(9,1)T[0,];
>
>   for(j in 1:n) {
>
>   for(i in offset[j]:(offset[j+1]-1)){
>
>   psi[1]<- log(pi[j,1])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[1], sigma);
>   psi[2]<- log(pi[j,2])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[2], sigma);
>   psi[3]<- log(pi[j,3])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[3], sigma);
>   psi[4]<- log(pi[j,4])+normal_log(Hb[i],beta[1]*Age[i]+beta[2]*Season[i]+beta[3]*TSPD[i]+theta1[4], sigma);
>
>    increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(psi));
>
>     }
> }

Given the truncation on theta1, you need to define it as:

   vector<lower=0>[k] theta1;

Once you do that, because it's given a normal(9,1) distribution,
it doesn't need the truncation (it's implicit in the declaration),
so you can more efficiently write:

  theta1 ~ normal(9,1);

We usually follow the convention of capitalizing size constants.

Is there a reason to bound sigma above at 1?

> Since in Stan the discrete distributions for the parameters are not possible, how can you define a distribution for the pi[j,c] (j=1,2,....,n), (c=1,2,3,4) that is probability for the person j belong to class c in above syntax? (In rjags, I used below codes).

I'm not sure what you mean here.  The pi as you wrote it in the above model
gets a uniform distribution over simplexes (that's proper because they're
bounded).  You can do inference using just the pi --- you don't need the
indicator variable g.  The normalization is done through the simplex definition.

Did you want to add some other kind of prior?

> Finally to identify gamma's in the below model, we have to constrain one of the classes's gammas to zero. How can we constrain a parameter to zero (or other values in Stan)?
> e.g.,
> gamma[1,1]<-0
> gamma[1,2]<-0
> gamma[1,3]<-0

You don't need to do this to identify in Stan.  It's implicit
in the way the simplex is defined.  What happens is that your
pi is a 4-simplex from the model's perspective, but is underlyingly
parameterized using 3 free parameters, so there's no problem with
identification of pi itself.

As with any mixture model, the indexes won't be clearly defined,
but there's not much we can do about that --- there's a discussion
in the manual in the problematic posteriors chapter.

>
>
> A part of syntax for rjags
> ################
> g[j] ~ dcat(psi[j,]) # Latent class indicator
>
> for(c in 1:4)
> {
> psi[j,c]<-phi[j,c]/sum(phi[j,])
> log(phi[j,c])<-gamma[c,1]+ gamma[c,2]*Age0[j]+gamma[c,3]*Hb0[j]
> }
> }
> ##########

Usually more is better than less here --- doesn't phi here
need to be given some kind of prior?

- Bob

 A part of syntax for rjags for model A
 ################
   for(j in 1:n) {

   g[j] ~ dcat(psi[j,]) # Latent class indicator

   pi[j,1:4]<-ddirch(1,1,1,1)
 }

A part of syntax for rjags for model B
 ################
   for(j in 1:n) {

   g[j] ~ dcat(psi[j,]) # Latent class indicator

 for(c in 1:4)
 {
 psi[j,c]<-phi[j,c]/sum(phi[j,])
 log(phi[j,c])<-gamma[c,1]+ gamma[c,2]*Age0[j]+gamma[c,3]*Hb0[j]
 }

##########

>  log(phi[j,c])<-gamma[c,1]+ gamma[c,2]*Age0[j]+gamma[c,3]*Hb0[j]
>  }
>  }

If you transpose the gammas, you can define psi without a loop as:

  psi[j] <- softmax(gamma[1] + gamma[2] * Age0[j] + gamma[3] * Hb0[j]);

The Stan notation gamma[2] is equivalent to R/JAGS/BUGS gamma[2,], and
now I'm assuming gamma is the transpose of what you have and that it's
defined as an array of vectors (or a matrix, though the array of vectors
is more efficient --- see the manual chapter on vectors vs. arrays).

But even better is to not bother with the softmax at all, and use
the logit-parameterized categorical, which would reduce all of the
above to just:

  for (j in 1:n)
    g[j] ~ categorical_logit(gamma[1] + gamma[2] * Age0[j] + gamma[3] * Hb0[j]);

- Bob

Sorry -- you're absolutely right.  Stan doesn't allow discrete parameters.
So instead,

  softmax(gamma[1] + gamma[2] * Age0[j] + gamma[3] * Hb0[j])

will give you the distribution over g on the linear scale.  You'll then
have to use that as in other mixture models for whatever you would've used
g for, but it looks like you had that sorted in the previous models.

- Bob

messages.subject: autocorrelation plots
messages.body_plain:
This is a mix of a simple question about rstan and a less simple
question of diagnostics.

It doesn't look as if rstan provides a way to graph the autocorrelations
over different lags.  Am I missing something?

If it's missing, is it missing because of doubts about the utility of
such plots?  My interest is in figuring how much thinning to do to get
it down to a "reasonable" level.

R already has other tools that can generate such plots for suitably
extracted coefficient values.  Of course, I have many chains and many
coefficients, which is perhaps one clue why the feature isn't there.
But I could identify the coefficient with the lowest n_eff and then look
at the plot for it.

My runs are currently sized to keep the minimum n_eff over 100. But
doubts about effective sample size for our final results (topic of my
previous post--thanks, Bob for the response) have led to an interest in
stretching out the chains to reduce the autocorrelations.

Originally I thought estimating the models would be slow but doing
simulations with them to estimate effects would be quick.  It turns out
the reverse is true, and so longer estimation runs aren't looking so bad
now.

Ross Boylan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] autocorrelation plots
messages.body_plain:
In most cases you should never need to look at the autocorrelation plots as the relevant info is incorporate into N_eff which is available
through all of the interfaces.  For example, if you generate 1000 samples but see N_eff = 100 then the natural thinning is 10.

As Mike notes thinning is a wasteful as you are literally throwing information away.  Geyer has a nice discussion in the Handbook of
MCMC (conveniently available for free, http://www.mcmchandbook.net/HandbookChapter1.pdf); he's an advocate of batches where
you average over a bin instead of taking a single sample.  Of course the problem there is that you're then stuck with the parameterization
of the chain and cannot compute the expectations of any nonlinear functions.

In the end thinning should be reserved for when you really do have huge autocorrelations and the output size becomes unmanageable
and only then.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

For overdispersed data negative binomial is commonly used.  I am currently working with overdispersed particle count data and the model analogous to salm fits quite well.  I am wondering if replacing
         y[dose,plate] ~ poisson(exp(alpha_star
                              + beta * centered_logx[dose]
                              + gamma * centered_x[dose]
                              + lambda[dose,plate]) );
with
         mu[dose,plate] <-alpha_star
                              + beta * centered_logx[dose]
                              + gamma * centered_x[dose]
                              + lambda[dose,plate];
         y[dose,plate] ~ neg_binomial(shape[dose], shape[dose]/exp(mu[dose,plate]) );

will do even better. What prior should I put on shape - gamma(0.001,0.001)?

I already tried using negative binomial for my problem but it didn't converge. After removing lambda it converged but then waic was higher than the one when using poisson. Any suggestions how to improve the model?

Thanks for help,
Linas

The key is that I don't know how to read in the 18 x 3 matrix in such a way that I can separate the missing and non-missing data without using NAs.

You need to also pass in an 18 x 3 binary array that is coded as 1 if the corresponding observation is observed and 0 if it is missing. I call this array R, BDA calls it I (although it is not an identity matrix), and some people reverse code it and call it M.

>  There appears to be a hint in this post <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/5KBr-xlunQM>, but the ultimate resolution wasn't clear enough for me to be able to implement it.  Can anyone help me to understand how to implement stan's missing data paradigm with multivariate data?

The paradigm is basically "don't have missing data". Failing that, you could modify the attachments to your case. The main points are
Pass in the R array so you know what is observed and what is missing (you also have to recode the missing values to be something like -999 for Stan to accept them but the -999 never actually gets used)
Declare the missing values as parameters to be estimated
In the model block, use the corresponding elements of R to make vectors that have a mix of observed data and proposed values for those that are missing originally
Call multi_normal_cholesky on those vectors (although it is better to use the onion method to create the Cholesky factor than to Cholesky factorize the covariance matrix)

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: a Waic example!
messages.body_plain:
On Apr 18, 2014, at 11:49 PM, Brian Hayden <bha...@lbl.gov> wrote:

> What is the difference between doing log_lik in the transformed parameters block and using increment_log_prob in the model block, versus doing it in a generated quantities block like this:
>
> generated quantities {
>     real log_lik;
>     log_lik <- 0;
>     for (n in 1:N){
>         log_lik <- log_lik + normal_log(y[n], X[n]*b, sigma);
>     }
> }
>
> I am asking mainly because I am trying to implement waic and I want to make sure the generated quantities version doesn't do something different.

They'll give you the same answer because Stan only cares about
the log probability function up to a constant as defined over
the parameters --- everything else is about what gets output.

So the two approaches will not give you a different answer.
But there are some subtle differences to what happens under the hood.

Transformed parameters are derived from parameters.  This means they
involve heavy automatic differentiation types.  This happens
every log prob evaluation, which is once per leapfrog step in
HMC/NUTS, which is roughly 2^treedepth per iteration.

Generated quantities are computed once per iteration using double
precision floating point values in C++ instead of auto-diff variables and
thus are faster to evaluate.

Another issue is that the function normal_log() does not drop constant
terms whereas the sampling statement version with ~ does.  We may clean
this all up in the future so they do the same thing or are ideally
configurable, but that's how it works now and it means a bit more overhead
for calling normal_log() than using sampling statements.     And if you
want to reuse these pieces to compute the log prob, then you have
to forego the built-in vectorization possibilities in the sampling
distributions.

Andrew prefers the generated quantities version because (a) it's faster,
and (b) it means the model can be written as it would be written if you weren't
computing WAIC.  In contrast, the transformed parameter approach is nice because
you only have to write the model once, even if it's coded a bit differently
than it would otherwise be coded.

This general advice is all buried in the manual in the description of
which variables get computed where.

You probably want an array of log likelihoods, one for each data
point, too.

- Bob

copy the bits of the model for them, or

(1 effective sampler per iteration), but it requires coding
the model twice.

messages.body_plain:
Working on NB regression modeling currently (not in Stan though, unfortunately), I got excited seeing the topic of this post!

Bob, if the development team is considering a direct parameterization of the NB distribution in terms of mean and dispersion, it'd be great to make a distinction between NB1 and NB2 parameterizations (Linus is using the latter), two commonly used alternatives in negative binomial regression (Cameron & Trivedi, Regression Analysis of Count Data, 2013):

NB1:
  y ~ poisson(lambda)
  lambda ~ gamma(mu/dispersion, dispersion)
  variance = mu + mu * dispersion = mu * (1 + dispersion)

NB2:
  y ~ poisson(lambda)
  lambda ~ gamma(1/dispersion, mu*dispersion)
  variance = mu + mu^2 * dispersion = mu * (1 + dispersion * mu)

Thanks,

Luc

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the careful report.

It looks like two issues.

1.  Negative results from poisson_rng are not by design.
I'm wondering if it's an overflow issue.  Any idea what the mean
fed into poisson_rng is that's causing the problem?

We should probably set up the RNGs to check for overflow
and throw exceptions.  There's no infinite value for ints the
way there is for real values.

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/625

Do you happen to have a reproducible seed and values for lot and mu that
cause the problem?  Ideally, just a simpler case not involving an array.

2.  The RNG issue, which assuming the parameterizations are all correct,
would be a separate bug.  I know there's been ongoing work on negative_binomial,
but all the parameterizations of that (and gamma) still make my head hurt.

I created an issue to investigate:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/626

- Bob

> On Wednesday, April 9, 2014 3:07:42 PM UTC-4, Ken Arnold wrote:
> > I'm experimenting with modeling correlation / covariance matrices with LKJ priors and it seems like a cool approach. But I'm encountering trouble when I try to scale up to higher dimensionality. In particular, even if I could get the model to run, the K-choose-2 factors will be increasingly hard to estimate as K gets large.
>
> This is something of a misconception. Yes, there are nominally K-choose-2 correlations to estimate but the volume of the sample space of K-dimensional correlation matrices shrinks for K > 6. In R, this is what you have to multiply by to get the density to integrate to 1
>
> constant <- function(K, eta = 1) {
>   if(K == 1) return(1)
>   k <- 1:(K-1)
>   log_constant <- -sum(k) / 2 * log(pi) + (K - 1) * lgamma(eta + (K-1)/2) -
>     sum(lgamma(eta + (K-k-1)/2))
>   return(exp(log_constant))
> }
> plot(sapply(1:43, constant), type = "l", log = "y", las = 1,
>      xlab = "K", ylab = "Constant")
>
>  <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-jvYG6wtPGDk/U0Web-lVZ0I/AAAAAAAAAOo/P5slF88MkiM/s1600/Rplot.png>
>
>
>
>
> > One approach I was thinking of is using a low-rank approximation, perhaps a truncated Cholesky decomposition. Has anyone tried this? What might be a good way to implement it in Stan?
>
> Short-rank correatlion matrices is one approach, but the first thing to try is the attachment, which generates the Cholesky factor, L, of a correlation matrix such that L * L' has a LKJ(eta) distribution. This will be much faster and avoid the numerical positive definiteness violations that you see.
>
> Making that Cholesky factor have more rows than columns is not terribly difficult but the distribution of the implied correlation matrix is not LKJ anymore. You would get larger correlations than under the LKJ prior with eta = 1, when typically you prefer smaller correlations (which can be accomplished under the LKJ prior by making eta > 1). On Monday, April 21, 2014 8:26:20 PM UTC-4, Ken Arnold wrote:
> Sorry for the delayed reply: this worked great! I was getting some nice results for kernel learning on top of this, but admittedly I was getting ahead of myself; a real presentation of results will have to wait until I get some other parts ironed out.

That would be interesting, possibly one of the coveted Models of the Week. I think the best way to do monster Gaussian process models is to use the onion method with eta = 1 to make L and pass that (possibly scaled) to multi_normal_cholesky(). Then L * L'  is distributed uniform over the correlation matrices, and you can put some sort of a distance-based prior on the correlations and wind that back through the Jacobians to the primitive parameters underlying L. If you instead construct the correlation matrix according to some covariance function and then try to take the Cholesky factorization of it, then you run into numerical problems or RAM limitations.

Ben

I'm having trouble getting a model implementing the guassian_dlm_obs likelihood to pull out the parameters from a synthetic dataset I've created. I can manually define a Gaussian dynamic linear model in Stan, and it resolves the parameters correctly, but the guassian_dlm_obs tends to overstate the parameter estimates by a significant amount. I've attached both Stan models, and the R code to create the fake data, and to run the two models (unfortunately, the manual model takes a "long" time to run compared to the native Stan implementation).

The synthetic model is a 500-observation univariate series generated by a univariate DLM regression model with 4 predictors and no intercept (i.e. the dimension of the state vector is 4). I've set the observation noise to be gaussian with mean 0, variance 1 and the system noise to be 4-dimensional gaussian with mean 0 and a covariance matrix equal to 0.1 * diag(4). So V = 1, and W = 0.1 * diag(4).

The quantiles corresponding to the posteriors under each of the two models are as follows (because both models learn W as a covariance matrix, there are really 10 parameters, but the off-diagonal entries are well-enough zero, and the draws for the diagonal entries are very similar):

guassian_dlm_obs:

V
2.5%   50%    97.5%
2.37     2.70     3.08

W
 2.5%     50%    97.5%
1.65      6.54     16.32

manual_dlm:

V
2.5%   50%    97.5%
0.91    0.97     1.04

W
 2.5%      50%    97.5%
 0.01      0.05       0.13

My R sessionInfo() output is as follows:

R version 3.0.2 (2013-09-25)
Platform: x86_64-apple-darwin10.8.0 (64-bit)

locale:
[1] en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8/C/en_US.UTF-8/en_US.UTF-8

attached base packages:
[1] parallel  stats     graphics  grDevices utils     datasets  methods   base

other attached packages:
[1] rstan_2.2.0      inline_0.3.13    Rcpp_0.11.1      mvtnorm_0.9-9997

loaded via a namespace (and not attached):
[1] codetools_0.2-8 stats4_3.0.2    tools_3.0.2

I'm wondering if I've used Stan's DLM implementation incorrectly. Any help would be greatly appreciated.

Thanks,
Rob

messages.subject: Speeding multilevel IRT
messages.body_plain:
I have a multi-level IRT model (graded response model for a Likert questionnaire) that seems to be converging quite slowly. The dataset involves ~6000 students in 5 countries, with 42 questions. I’m modeling effects of sex and religion, allowing the effects to vary by country.  There are enough moving parts here that it may just be that I have to accept long run times to get convergence, but if anyone has advice on how to speed this up, I’d appreciate it. The model seems to need at least 500 iterations for good convergence, which takes a day or so to run 3 parallel chains on my 4-core 2.8 GHz i7 Macbook. Anything that could cut that time down would be great.

I also wonder whether I’m handling the multi-level modeling of sex and religion right. I feel like I ought to be modeling the group-level variations using a covariance matrix as discussed in section 9.9 of the manual (and Chapter 13 of Gelman and Hill), but I can’t quite figure out how to make that work with categorical variables like sex and religion.  Is it necessary (or meaningful) to be working from a covariance matrix for such variables anyway, or is the system I have here OK?

Many thanks,
Josh

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Multi-level Bayesian Framework using Arrays of Different Dimensions
messages.body_plain:
We've been planning to add ragged arrays, but haven't yet.
The C++ structure for arrays is a std::vector, so there's
no problem modifying it for ragged arrays.  Sparse vectors
and matrices will eventually be added as new basic datatypes,
along with other structured types (next to be rolled out is
Cholesky factor for correlation matrices).

We should make it clearer in the manual(s) that we don't
support them now --- as is, it's only implicit in that the enumeration
of things we do support are all non-ragged.

In the manual, in the chapter on clustering, in the section on naive Bayes,
there's a subsection titled "Representing Ragged Arrays in Stan".
This is the kind of organization Herra Huu is suggesting.
We also use it for things like IRT models when not every
student gets every question on the test or Bradley-Terry
models for non-round-robin tournaments.  And you can use
it for sparse matrices, as well, but we don't yet support
any sparse matrix operations.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] discrete missing data
messages.body_plain:
Stan doesn't support discrete parameters, so there's no easy way
to do a missing data model with discrete parameters.  The best you
can hope for is being able to marginalize out the missing discrete
parameters.  Or to change the model to use continuous parameters.

Using a continuous parameter and rounding it is not a good idea, nor
is any operation that introduces discontinuities in output that's used
in the overall log probability calculation.  It breaks the gradient's
connection to the log prob and causes HMC to devolve to a random walk.
We haven't experimented much with such an approach, but we're also worried
about the interaction with adaptation and the continuous sampling for
the other parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Speeding multilevel IRT
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure about the modeling issues, but for efficiency,
you want to take loops like this:

  for (i in 1:C) {
    gamma_raw_c[i]~normal(gamma_raw,sigma_gamma_c[i]);
    beta_c[i]~normal(beta,sigma_beta_c[i]);
  }

and vectorize them to:

  gamma_raw_c ~ normal(gamma_raw, sigma_gamma_c);
  beta_c ~ normal(beta, sigma_beta_c);

It won't be a huge speed improvement because the scales vary.

For an IRT model, this parameterization

  for (n in 1:N) {
    p[n] <- (gamma_c[cc[jj[n]],kk[n]]) *(alpha[jj[n]]
              -beta_c[cc[jj[n]],kk[n]] +delta );
    y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(p[n],c[kk[n]]);
  }

is confusing me.  You use jj for indexes all around.  Shouldn't
there be students and questiosn with separate indexing?

The usual IRT model would be:

  gamma[j] * (alpha[i] - beta[j])

where gamma is discriminativeness and beta difficulty for problem
j and alpha is ability for student i.  An easier-to-sample-from parameterization
is:

 (gamma[j] * alpha[i]) - beta2[j]

where you can recover beta = beta2 ./ gamma (elementwise divide).

The usual problems for these models is identifiability.
So you want to make sure the priors are strong enough or
particular items are fixed in value.

- Bob

Identification seems to be working well. In the reparameterization below, I’d probably keep delta inside the parentheses and let it be mu_alpha, holding mu_beta at 0.

I’ll be interested to test the effects of vectorizing the country-level sampling statements and reparameterizing the IRT model.

I assume there’s no way to effect the Matt trick here?

On Apr 24, 2014, at 6:20 PM, Joshua Rosenau <josh.r...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks.  The use of jj for indexes is because I'm allowing item parameters to vary by country. So gamma_c and beta_c are indexed by country (a property of the individual, hence indexed with jj) and by item (indexed kk).

I rescale the person parameters by dividing out the sd of the computed values after accounting for the multi-level hierarchy, thus controlling multiplicative nonidentification, and the location priors/hyperpriors on alpha and beta is set to 0, with the offset delta modeled separately. In the reparameterization below, I'd probably keep delta inside the parentheses and let it be mu_alpha, holding mu_beta at 0.

Andrew and Jennifer suggest that in their regression book, but we don't recommend
it with HMC.  The problem is that the model's still unidentified on the space over
which sampling is happening, which makes it hard for adaptation to find a reasonable
scale.

>
> I'll be interested to test the effects of vectorizing the country-level sampling statements and reparameterizing the IRT model.
>
> I assume there's no way to effect the Matt trick here?

You could do that with the parameters.  If you have a lot of data, it's probably
not necessary, but if the data sizes used for estimating any of the coefficients
is small, then going to the uncentered (Matt trick) parameterization would probably
help, too.  We haven't experimented with it for IRT specifically (as far as I know), so
I'd be interested in hearing the results.

- Bob

> On Apr 24, 2014, at 8:54 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
>> I'm not sure about the modeling issues, but for efficiency,
>> you want to take loops like this:
>>
>> for (i in 1:C) {
>>   gamma_raw_c[i]~normal(gamma_raw,sigma_gamma_c[i]);
>>   beta_c[i]~normal(beta,sigma_beta_c[i]);
>> }
>>
>> and vectorize them to:
>>
>> gamma_raw_c ~ normal(gamma_raw, sigma_gamma_c);
>> beta_c ~ normal(beta, sigma_beta_c);
>>
>> It won't be a huge speed improvement because the scales vary.
>>
>> For an IRT model, this parameterization
>>
>> for (n in 1:N) {
>>   p[n] <- (gamma_c[cc[jj[n]],kk[n]]) *(alpha[jj[n]]
>>             -beta_c[cc[jj[n]],kk[n]] +delta );
>>   y[n] ~ ordered_logistic(p[n],c[kk[n]]);
>> }
>>
>> is confusing me.  You use jj for indexes all around.  Shouldn't
>> there be students and questiosn with separate indexing?
>>
>> The usual IRT model would be:
>>
>> gamma[j] * (alpha[i] - beta[j])
>>
>> where gamma is discriminativeness and beta difficulty for problem
>> j and alpha is ability for student i.  An easier-to-sample-from parameterization
>> is:
>>
>> (gamma[j] * alpha[i]) - beta2[j]
>>
>> where you can recover beta = beta2 ./ gamma (elementwise divide).
>>
>> The usual problems for these models is identifiability.
>> So you want to make sure the priors are strong enough or
>> particular items are fixed in value.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>
>> On Apr 24, 2014, at 7:27 AM, Joshua Rosenau <josh.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>>> I have a multi-level IRT model (graded response model for a Likert questionnaire) that seems to be converging quite slowly. The dataset involves ~6000 students in 5 countries, with 42 questions. I'm modeling effects of sex and religion, allowing the effects to vary by country.  There are enough moving parts here that it may just be that I have to accept long run times to get convergence, but if anyone has advice on how to speed this up, I'd appreciate it. The model seems to need at least 500 iterations for good convergence, which takes a day or so to run 3 parallel chains on my 4-core 2.8 GHz i7 Macbook. Anything that could cut that time down would be great.
>>>
>>> I also wonder whether I'm handling the multi-level modeling of sex and religion right. I feel like I ought to be modeling the group-level variations using a covariance matrix as discussed in section 9.9 of the manual (and Chapter 13 of Gelman and Hill), but I can't quite figure out how to make that work with categorical variables like sex and religion.  Is it necessary (or meaningful) to be working from a covariance matrix for such variables anyway, or is the system I have here OK?
>>>
>>> Many thanks,
>>> Josh

messages.subject: PyStan and Mavericks
messages.body_plain:
Just in case anybody has been running into issues, there is a known conflict in the latest version
of Mavericks that has been causing all kinds of problems with Python installs.  Fortunately the
workaround is pretty easy, although you won’t be able to use pip.

All you really have to do is make sure that you set

export ARCHFLAGS=-Wno-error=unused-command-line-argument-hard-error-in-future

is set in the local environment when you compile and run PyStan.  Be careful with any sudo’ing
that you might do, as this creates a new environment that won’t recognize any local exports.

So, for example,

git clone g...@github.com:stan-dev/pystan.git
sudo ARCHFLAGS=-Wno-error=unused-command-line-argument-hard-error-in-future python setup.py install
export ARCHFLAGS=-Wno-error=unused-command-line-argument-hard-error-in-future
python
...proceed with Stan’ing…

Word on the street is that a new release of Mavericks with a consistent Python install is coming soon,
but this should provide a reasonable workaround for the time being.

If you run into any other issues let us know.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] declaration of variables in 'transformed parameters' block
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] declaration of variables in 'transformed parameters' block
messages.body_plain:
You don't need to put all locals at the top of a loop.  You
can just have a standalone nested block, as in:

model {
   ... lots of priors ...

   {
     vector[N] y_hat;
     y_hat <- X * beta;
     y ~ normal(y_hat, sigma);
   }
}

And this makes y_hat local in its block.

The best place to look for behaviors is the language reference,
or roughly the second half of the manual.  There's a section
"Statement Blocks and Local Variable Declarations" that describes
how variables come to be local.  What's particularly confusing is
that the model block is treated as a statement block --- that's described
in the "Program block: model" section.

I made a note to clarify that in the next version of the manual as part of
the next manual issue:

  https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/567

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> Cambridge, MA is awesome (even if it is based on Cambridge, UK).

I was only teasing!  I did my grad work in Cambridge (MA) and now that I’m working
in London I feel like I have to represent.  But we’re all Cantabrigians at heart.

> Burn-in was based on model convergence and chain mixing.  This will vary with models and datasets.  The suggestion to start smaller is very sensible and the 50k is likely overkill.  Some of my more recent SEMs - albeit much simpler and with less data - are converging in under 5k.

For relatively simple models (such as most of the BUGS models) only short warmups are needed — HMC
tends to converge very, very quickly.  Harder models will, of course, require more warm up, both to ensure
convergence but also to ensure good adaptation of the metric.

Start with half and then keep increasing it until the samples are consistent with convergence (as judged
by Rhat, for example).

> I remember reading somewhere in Stan documentation that at least four chains was recommended.  But again, my decision was based on convergence and chain mixing.  I found that this worked better and faster with more smaller chains than three long ones.

4 is the default in PyStan and RStan, and it was chosen because it’s better than 2 and less expensive than 6…
Seriously, though, you want enough chains that you have a reasonable probability of finding any extra modes
or any pathological regions of phase space.  4 has worked well in practice, but if you have extra cores then
feel free to add more — more chains is always better.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] speedup tip for binomial_logit
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure why binomial_logit would be a lot slower
than the normal.  Could you share the rest of your model?

The normal is particularly easy to evaluate with fixed deviation
on the log scale --- it's just subtraction and multiplications/division.

I'd think the normal would be a good approximation with counts of
100 if the success probability isn't too close to 0 or 1.
You can just fit the deviation --- that would give you the equivalent
of overdispersion in the binomial.  You need to be careful with
logit(1) and logit(0) as they produce +inf and -inf.

There's also the Poisson approximation to large
binomials and negative binomial for overdispersion.

- Bob

Is it possible to do that in Stan?

I'm not sure what kind of point estimation WinBUGS does.  Packages
like Coda summarize the posterior with sample means and medians.
We do not have summaries that include covariance.  We probably should
provide that option.  It's easy to produce in R once you have the samples,

>

The manual has a chapter on coding missing data.  Stan cannot directly
handle the R NA format that BUGS/JAGS can.

- Bob

Daniel

However, I'm not quite certain what parameters I should estimate and which statistical modeling I will need to use in Stan. What I do want to know from the parameter estimates is that whether or not, say categorical variable X is independent of another category Y.

Thanks.

and in case you miss the background:

  http://andrewgelman.com/2009/05/15/i_hate_the_so-c/
